Ensure continued business justification, because the employers' pledges are the main source of the project's benefits.
Learn from experience, because the wind operators already train apprentices and can pass on lessons from their own centres.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: The principle now covers relationships as well as roles: the project management team initiates and builds relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (see manual 2.3). A regular group that helps the employers and the college understand each other and agree who contacts whom does exactly that.

n.1: The group exists to build understanding and agree contacts, not to write product descriptions or quality specifications.
n.2: The pledges matter to the business case, but the action described is building relationships, not checking that the project is still justified.
n.3: Nothing in the group's purpose is about seeking or recording lessons; it is about relationships and engagement.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is at the end of the detailed design and procurement stage, and the design-and-build contract is about to be signed. To save board time, Mark Ostrowski proposes treating stages 3, 4 and 5 as a single 13-month stage running to the opening day, because the contractor's programme covers all of that work. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because longer stages reduce the burden on senior managers, and the contractor's programme has been agreed.
It applies it well, because the board will still receive highlight reports and can step in if a problem arises.
It applies it poorly, because a 13-month stage removes the points where the board reviews viability before committing more.
It applies it poorly, because commissioning and handover should be planned as part of a separate closing stage.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Manage by stages gives the board review and decision points at which it assesses viability before authorizing the next stage; shorter stages give more control, longer ones less burden (see manual 2.4). Merging the structural, fit-out and handover stages leaves no point between signing the contract and opening day at which the board decides whether to continue, despite the tight cost limit.

n.0: Stage length is a trade-off, but on a large build with a 3% cost limit and a fixed date, one 13-month stage gives up too much control; the contractor's programme does not replace board decision points.
n.1: Highlight reports keep the board informed, but they are not decision points at which the board reviews viability and authorizes the next commitment.
n.3: Closing a project is not a stage; it is the last part of the final stage, so commissioning and handover cannot move into a closing stage.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The governors' limit of 3% above the approved budget and the fixed September opening are recorded as project tolerances. The board sets cost and time tolerances for each stage, Leah Whitfield agrees to raise an exception report as soon as a stage is forecast to go beyond them, and Mark Ostrowski will refer any forecast beyond the project tolerances to the governors. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by stages, because the board sets separate cost and time tolerances for each of the five stages.
Ensure continued business justification, because a forecast overspend beyond 3% would threaten the college's reserves.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because Leah and Mark each have a defined part in escalating problems.
Manage by exception, because each level has limits of delegated authority and forecast breaches are escalated to the next level.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Manage by exception sets limits of delegated authority through tolerances, with escalation to the next level as soon as a breach is forecast: the business layer sets project tolerances, the board stage tolerances, and exceptions go upwards (see manual 2.5 and 11.2.1).

n.0: Tolerances are set per stage, but setting limits of authority and escalating forecast breaches is manage by exception.
n.1: An overspend would affect justification, but the arrangement described sets limits of delegated authority and escalation routes.
n.2: Roles are involved, but the core of the arrangement is tolerances at each level and escalation when they are forecast to be exceeded.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Before the architect starts the detailed design, Leah Whitfield arranges for Bethany Cole, Craig Dunmore and the architect to write the product description for the welding bays together. It sets out what each bay contains, the fume extraction performance it must achieve and who will review and approve it. How well does this apply the 'focus on products' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because Craig Dunmore holds a health and safety qualification and can approve the fume extraction design.
It applies it well, because defining each product and its quality requirements before design guides the work and avoids waste.
It applies it poorly, because product descriptions should be written by the supplier once the contract has been awarded.
It applies it poorly, because the vice principal's request for 30 bays must be decided before any product description is written.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Focus on products means defining products and their quality expectations before the work, so that the project is output-oriented and does no more than needed; product descriptions give purpose, composition, quality specifications and approval responsibilities, and co-creating them with users helps adoption (see manual 2.6 and 3.5.1).

n.0: Who approves is set out in the product description itself; Craig's qualification does not explain why defining the product first is good practice.
n.2: Product descriptions are prepared when planning, with input from users and suppliers; waiting for the contractor would leave the design without agreed requirements.
n.3: A request for change is handled through issue control; it does not stop the bays being described now, and the description can be updated if a change is approved.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Leah Whitfield proposes calling the project board the 'Skills Centre Steering Group', as the college names its capital project boards, using the college's capital project report template for highlight reports, and adding a site safety section to every highlight report, as one governor has asked. How well does this apply the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the method can use the college's terms and formats and report the risks that matter here.
It applies it well, because tailoring lets the college set aside the principles that do not suit a building project.
It applies it poorly, because PRINCE2 names should be kept so that everyone can recognize the roles and products.
It applies it poorly, because tailoring is decided by the business layer before the project manager is appointed.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's environment and risk: terminology can follow the organization's own, management products can take different formats, and controls such as reporting are shaped to the project's needs, here the safety risk next to the student entrance (see manual 2.7). The decisions are documented in the PID for the board to approve.

n.1: Principles cannot be tailored away; tailoring adapts processes, practices, roles, products and terminology.
n.2: Using the organization's own terminology is a recognized form of tailoring.
n.3: The project manager leads 'agree the tailoring requirements' in initiation, and the board approves the result in the PID.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. The curriculum team designs courses in the main college building, while the contractor's site team, the Danish rig installers and Leah Whitfield, who works three days a week, are seldom on site together. Misunderstandings about room layouts are growing. Leah sets up a fortnightly site walk-round and lunch for Bethany Cole, the site manager and the installers, with a shared online board for questions in between. Is this an appropriate approach to leading the team, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager's role is to instruct each team on how its tasks should be carried out.
Yes, because regular purposeful contact builds trust and social cohesion between groups that rarely work together.
No, because the curriculum team belongs to the user community and so is not part of the project team.
No, because the contractor's staff work for their own company and so are outside Leah's leadership.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Bringing teams together means optimizing people's time and building social cohesion: people meeting purposefully and regularly, building trust across project silos; teams that are not co-located need deliberate methods to achieve this (see manual 3.3.3).

n.0: Instructing tasks is management; the action here is building trust and cohesion between groups, which is leadership.
n.2: People who use the products contribute to the project; the curriculum team is doing project work on the courses.
n.3: Leading across organizational boundaries is part of leading project teams; it calls for cultural intelligence, not exclusion.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Mark Ostrowski proposes that Craig Dunmore's estates team administer the design-and-build contract and check the contractor's monthly valuations, as they manage the college's small works contracts. Leah Whitfield notes that nobody in the team has handled a contract above £200,000, while Hamish Grant's firm checks valuations on large projects. Is this an appropriate approach to building the team, and why?
o: Yes, because the estates team will look after the building once it opens and so should own the contract.
Yes, because the college is acting as a thick client and should do most of the project work itself.
No, because contract administration is a project support task and so cannot be given to user representatives.
No, because roles should match capability, and the gap should be closed by upskilling or by giving the work to others.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Roles should reflect capability, authority and availability; the project manager identifies competency gaps and mitigates them, for example by upskilling or by shifting responsibilities to more suitable people, such as the cost consultant who already checks valuations (see manual 3.3.2).

n.0: Looking after the building later does not give the team the capability to administer a large contract now.
n.1: A thick client does much of the work itself, but roles should still go to people with the capability to fill them.
n.2: Contract tasks are not reserved to project support; the problem is the capability gap, not who the team represents.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Tenders show the budget is tight, and Mark Ostrowski suggests replacing the nacelle rig with a cheaper computer simulator. Before any recommendation goes to the board, Leah Whitfield meets Ade Okafor and the other wind operator to understand what their apprentices must be able to do on a real rig and how a simulator would affect their pledges. Is this an appropriate way to lead change with the people affected, and why?
o: Yes, because the wind operators are key influencers whose pledges rest on the rig, so their needs should shape the decision.
Yes, because the employers are paying for the rig and so have the authority to approve or reject the change.
No, because employers outside the college are not project stakeholders and can be informed after the board has decided.
No, because the change is a request for change, which the board decides without consulting stakeholders.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Stakeholder engagement means identifying stakeholders and key influencers and building relationships so that all impacted areas are involved as the project progresses (see manual 3.2.2). The wind operators say the rig is the main reason they are committing apprentices, so their needs should shape any recommendation.

n.1: The rig is funded by the grant and college reserves; the employers have influence, not authority over project decisions.
n.2: Stakeholders include organizations outside the business that can affect or be affected by the project; the employers are key ones.
n.3: Assessing a change is best done cooperatively; understanding its effect on stakeholders informs the recommendation to the board.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. Three of the college's current electrical instructors, who will move into the new centre, keep objecting to the planned teaching timetable and have stopped attending design workshops. Sunita Rao suggests leaving them out of the remaining workshops so that decisions can be made faster. Is this an appropriate way to lead the change, and why?
o: Yes, because co-creation works best with people who support the change and will promote it to others.
Yes, because the instructors' line manager can direct them to accept the timetable once the centre opens.
No, because their resistance shows where engagement is needed, so the reasons behind it should be explored.
No, because each instructor is a senior user and must approve the course timetable before the centre opens.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Pockets of resistance show where communication and engagement should be focused: find out why people resist rather than sidelining them, and involve users in co-creating the ways of working they will adopt (see manual 3.2 and 3.4).

n.0: Co-creation involves users and key influencers, including doubters; excluding them makes adoption less likely.
n.1: Directing people to comply does not deal with the cause of resistance or help them move to the target state.
n.3: The instructors are users, but they do not hold the senior user role; Sunita Rao represents the users on the board.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is about to start the asbestos removal and strip-out. Site traffic will use a new gate, and the student pedestrian route will move for four months. About 1,800 students aged 16 to 18 use the main campus each day, and many arrive by bus. Leah Whitfield is updating the communication management approach. Which action BEST applies it?
o: Ask the main contractor to post notices on the site hoarding, as it is responsible for safety on its own site.
Plan messages for students, parents and bus operators through channels they use, with a way to raise concerns.
Add the route change to the next highlight report, so that the board and governors know about it first.
Send one email to all students and staff from the principal on the day before the strip-out starts.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: The communication management approach sets the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, each stakeholder group, based on stakeholder analysis of who is affected (see manual 3.4). Students, parents and bus operators are directly affected by the moved route, so messages should reach them through suitable channels before and during the work, with a way to respond.

n.0: Site notices reach people who are already at the site; they do not plan messages for each affected group or allow feedback.
n.2: The highlight report informs the board about stage status; it does not reach the students and others who are affected.
n.3: A single late message with no route for feedback does not give a controlled, two-way flow of information.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Leah Whitfield drafts this entry for the communication management approach: 'Rachel Tse, sustainability manager: reports on the climate targets to the governors and the combined authority; strong influence on grant compliance scoring; worried that the heat pumps could be cut to save money.' Under which heading should this entry be recorded, and why?
o: Communications schedule and procedures, because it sets out how Rachel will report to the combined authority.
Supporting tools and techniques, because Rachel uses reporting tools to track the climate emergency targets.
Stakeholder analysis, because it records who is affected by or can influence the project and their current views.
Resources, because Rachel's time is needed for the project's communication activities on sustainability.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is impacted by the project's outcome or delivery and who can influence its success or failure, with their interests and concerns (see manual 3.4). Rachel's role, influence on grant scoring and concern about the heat pumps belong there; the schedule and procedures then plan the messages for her.

n.0: The entry does not set out when or how messages will be sent; it describes Rachel's interest, influence and position.
n.1: No tool or platform for communication is described; the entry is about a stakeholder.
n.3: The entry does not commit Rachel's time to communication work; it analyses her as a stakeholder.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Wenmoor's single point of access (SPA) project is at the boundary between the Eastfield pilot stage and the evaluation and roll-out stage. The commissioner has just confirmed that it will no longer withhold contract value if the SPA is late, and pilot data show referral to first contact falling to seven days, not the three days in the business case. Karen Lindqvist, the executive, says that because staff are trained and much of the budget is spent, the roll-out should go ahead without revisiting the business case. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because stopping after the pilot would waste the money already spent on backfill and training.
It applies it well, because the executive owns the business case and decides when it needs to be reviewed.
It applies it poorly, because the benefits should be confirmed in a post-project review before the roll-out is authorized.
It applies it poorly, because the business case should be checked at the stage boundary to confirm the roll-out is still worth doing.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: The justification for a project must remain valid and be revalidated throughout, and the board checks the business case at every stage boundary before authorizing the next stage (see manual 2.1 and 5.3.1). A change in the contract position and a much weaker benefit forecast are exactly what that check is for; if the roll-out is no longer justified it should be changed or stopped.

n.0: Money already spent cannot be recovered whatever is decided; the decision should rest on whether the remaining investment is still justified by the remaining benefits.
n.1: The executive is accountable for the business case, but that accountability includes having it checked at each stage end, not skipping the check.
n.2: Benefits are mainly confirmed after closure; at a stage boundary the business case is updated and checked using forecasts, not confirmed.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Ellie Chandran, the project manager, finds that nobody recorded why the 2021 attempt to introduce central booking in Moorside was abandoned. She arranges to talk to Gareth Pugh, who took part in it, and to the managers of another community health provider that already runs a single point of access, and she records what she learns in the lessons log. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because Gareth Pugh is an informal leader whose support the project will need.
Ensure continued business justification, because the 2021 failure suggests the board must prove the SPA is worth doing.
Learn from experience, because lessons are being sought from an earlier attempt and from another organization.
Manage by stages, because the 2021 attempt ran for four months without a point at which it could be reviewed.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Learn from experience: lessons are sought, recorded and acted on from the start of a project, and where an organization has little relevant experience it is even more important to learn from others, including outside organizations (see manual 2.2). Consulting people with experience of similar work and recording it in the lessons log is the 'assess previous lessons' activity (13.4.2).

n.0: Gareth's influence matters for engaging Moorside nurses, but here Ellie is drawing on his experience of the earlier attempt, not defining his role or relationships.
n.1: Ellie is collecting lessons, not testing whether the SPA is desirable, viable and achievable; its justification rests on the commissioner's condition and the expected benefits.
n.3: The scenario does not say how the 2021 attempt was controlled; Ellie's action is seeking and recording lessons, not dividing this project into stages.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the 'starting up a project' process. Karen Lindqvist, the executive, first proposes Moira Healy, head of nursing for Eastfield, as the only senior user. Moira points out that she has no authority over the Moorside and Holtby nursing teams, which will have to change how they work during the roll-out. Karen therefore also appoints the heads of nursing for Moorside and Holtby as senior users. How well does this apply the 'define roles, responsibilities and relationships' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because users in all three localities are represented by people with authority over the teams affected.
It applies it well, because a larger board shares the executive's accountability for the project among more people.
It applies it poorly, because a project board should have a single senior user so that user decisions are not delayed.
It applies it poorly, because Gareth Pugh, whose views many Moorside nurses follow, should be their senior user.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: The principle requires a project management team in which the business, user and supplier interests are properly represented by people with the authority to commit their area (see manual 2.3 and 6.2.1). The senior user role can be held by more than one person, so adding the Moorside and Holtby heads of nursing gives every locality that must adopt the SPA a voice in directing it.

n.1: There is one executive, whose accountability cannot be shared or delegated; adding senior users does not change that.
n.2: The senior user role can be shared by several people; leaving two localities unrepresented would weaken user commitment to the roll-out.
n.3: Gareth is a key influencer to engage, but he is an informal leader rather than the manager of the Moorside teams; the senior user needs authority to commit user resources.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Moira Healy, head of nursing for Eastfield, says her team is overstretched and asks to open the triage hub in Eastfield now, using draft triage criteria, rather than wait for the project to be authorized. Karen Lindqvist, the executive, agrees so that benefits start sooner, and asks Ellie Chandran to finish the project initiation documentation alongside. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because an early start in Eastfield will give the board real data with which to judge the business case.
It applies it well, because the senior user may start using products in her own locality once she judges them fit.
It applies it poorly, because delivery work should not begin until the board has authorized the project and the next stage.
It applies it poorly, because each stage should be the same length so that the board reviews the project at regular intervals.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Manage by stages makes sure a project is properly initiated before delivery work starts, and each stage begins when the board authorizes it (see manual 2.4 and 14.4.4). Opening the hub during initiation, with criteria that have not been signed off, bypasses that decision point in a trust with a low appetite for clinical safety risk.

n.0: Pilot data are useful, but the plan already provides a controlled Eastfield pilot after the design stage; wanting data does not justify skipping the authorization decision.
n.1: The senior user accepts products against agreed criteria but has no authority to start delivery; work begins when the project and the stage are authorized.
n.3: Stage lengths vary with risk, complexity and decision points; the SPA plan already has stages of 8, 12, 16 and 24 weeks.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the Eastfield pilot stage. Ellie Chandran authorizes the triage hub work package with tolerances of three days and £4,000. Within those limits, the team manager, the hub's lead nurse, decides how to cover rota gaps and reports this in her weekly checkpoint report; if she forecasts that the limits will be exceeded, she raises it with Ellie straight away. How well does this apply the 'manage by exception' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the team manager reports the hub's progress to the project manager at regular intervals.
It applies it well, because authority is delegated within tolerances to the people who know the work, and forecast breaches are escalated.
It applies it poorly, because rota decisions during the pilot should be referred to the project board, which is accountable for it.
It applies it poorly, because the work package should also carry a benefits tolerance to protect the three-day target.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Manage by exception sets limits of delegated authority through tolerances, so each level decides within its limits and escalates as soon as a breach is forecast (see manual 2.5 and 11.2.1). Decisions are best made at the most local level where the knowledge sits (3.5.1): here the lead nurse decides rota cover and raises a forecast breach with the project manager.

n.0: Regular checkpoint reporting is time-driven progress control; it does not explain the delegation within tolerances and escalation on which manage by exception relies.
n.2: The board manages by exception; day-to-day decisions inside the work package belong to the team manager, within the tolerances the project manager has set.
n.3: Work package tolerances cover scope, cost and time; a benefits tolerance is not set in a work package description.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Before any triage criteria are drafted, Ellie Chandran and Moira Healy meet nurses and therapists from all three localities to agree a description of the 'triage criteria' product: what it is for, what it must contain, and that every criterion must be signed off by the clinical safety officer and the medical director before use. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Focus on products, because the team is agreeing what the triage criteria must contain and the quality they must meet before work starts.
Tailor to suit the project, because the clinical sign-off is a trust rule added to the standard PRINCE2 method for this project.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the description names who must approve the triage criteria.
Manage by exception, because the clinical safety officer's sign-off limits what the triage hub may change by itself.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Focus on products: the project defines its products, including their purpose, composition and quality requirements, before doing the work, so that the work delivers what users need and no more (see manual 2.6). Writing the product description with staff from every locality also co-creates the product, which helps adoption (3.5.1).

n.1: The sign-off rule is a quality requirement written into the product description, not an adaptation of the method to suit the project.
n.2: Naming approvers is one part of a product description; the action as a whole is defining the product before it is built.
n.3: Manage by exception concerns tolerances and escalation between management levels; an approval requirement for a product is part of defining that product.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Ellie Chandran proposes that project documents use the trust's own term 'senior responsible owner' for the executive role, and that highlight reports become a one-page summary posted fortnightly on the trust's collaboration platform, where board members can comment, because most of them work on rotas and meet online at lunchtime. Is this appropriate tailoring, and why?
o: Yes, because terminology and the format of reports can be adapted to the trust while the controls they provide are kept.
Yes, because tailoring allows the board to drop highlight reports when its members can see progress on the platform.
No, because PRINCE2 role names must be used in all project documents so that the method is applied consistently.
No, because the board should meet in person at each reporting interval to review the highlight report together.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Tailoring adapts the method to the project's environment and people: the organization's own terms can replace PRINCE2 terms, and the format and frequency of reports can suit the way the board works, while the principles and the controls the reports provide are kept (see manual 2.7). A short online highlight report suits a dispersed board that works on rotas.

n.1: The proposal keeps highlight reports and changes their format; it does not remove the time-driven reporting control.
n.2: Using the organization's own terms is a recognized form of tailoring; what cannot be tailored away are the principles.
n.3: PRINCE2 does not require the board to meet in person to receive highlight reports; virtual reporting to a dispersed board is acceptable tailoring.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Design team members work part-time or on rotas across the three localities and meet online at lunchtime. Ellie Chandran notices that Moorside and Eastfield staff rarely build on each other's ideas. She arranges a half-day design workshop each month, held in each locality in turn, for the key designers, with their clinical time backfilled from the budget, while keeping the short online meetings. Is this an appropriate way to lead the team, and why?
o: Yes, because co-located teams share information more easily, so the design team should now be moved to one site.
Yes, because a dispersed, part-time team needs deliberate chances to meet so that trust and cohesion can form.
No, because team-building is a matter for the line managers in each locality rather than for the project manager.
No, because the backfill budget pays for clinical time and should not be used for workshops away from patients.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Virtual, remote or hybrid teams do not build social cohesion by chance: deliberate methods, such as regular and purposeful in-person sessions for key people, build trust across project silos (see manual 3.3.3). Building the temporary project team is part of leading it, so Ellie is right to arrange this.

n.0: The workshops are held in each locality in turn and the team keeps working in its own localities; nobody is being moved to one site.
n.2: Leading and building the temporary project team is part of the project manager's and the board's responsibility; line managers do not lead the project team.
n.3: The workshops release clinicians from patient work, which is what backfilling clinical time pays for.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Hub nurses complain that Medivault's configuration team does not understand clinical language, and Medivault says the nurses' requests are vague. Ellie Chandran arranges for two Medivault configurers to spend a day in the Eastfield referral office, and for nurses to join Medivault's planning sessions, so that each side learns how the other works. Is this an appropriate way to lead the team, and why?
o: Yes, because leading across organizational boundaries depends on understanding how each organization works.
Yes, because the senior supplier is accountable for the quality of the products that the supplier delivers.
No, because Medivault is a contracted supplier, so working practices should be set by its support contract.
No, because the configurers' time should go on configuration work rather than on visits to the referral office.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Projects bring together people from different organizations with different cultures; leading across those boundaries calls for cultural intelligence, the ability to relate to and work across those cultures (see manual 3.3.1). Letting each side see how the other works builds shared understanding and better working relationships.

n.1: This is true of the senior supplier, but it does not explain why the joint visits help the two teams work together.
n.2: A contract sets what is supplied, but the project still has to build working relationships across organizations; the contract does not resolve misunderstandings between the teams.
n.3: Time spent understanding the users' work reduces rework from misunderstood requests; it supports the configuration rather than competing with it.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Many Moorside district nurses believe the triage hub will remove their professional judgement about which patients they see first. Gareth Pugh, a senior district nurse whose views many of them follow, shares this concern. Ellie Chandran invites Gareth to co-lead the working group that designs the triage criteria for rural visits. Is this an appropriate way to lead the change, and why?
o: Yes, because Gareth's long service makes him the right person to be the senior user for the Moorside locality.
Yes, because involving a key influencer in designing the new ways of working helps the people affected to adopt them.
No, because Gareth holds no formal role, so the project should work with Moorside nurses through their line managers.
No, because the loss of control over referrals is a dis-benefit already in the business case, so it has been accepted.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Leading change means identifying key influencers, including people with no formal role, and co-creating products and ways of working with users and influencers so that they are adopted (see manual 3.2.2 and 3.3). Giving Gareth a real part in designing rural triage can turn a likely source of resistance into ownership.

n.0: The action is about co-creating the criteria, not about board roles; the senior user needs authority to commit user resources, which an informal leader does not hold.
n.2: Projects should involve key people who are critical to success even when they hold no formal role; line management alone will not address an informal leader's influence.
n.3: Recording a dis-benefit in the business case does not remove the need to lead the people affected through the change.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. Several Moorside GP practices say they will keep faxing referrals to the nurses they know, and Dr Anita Kapoor, chair of the Moorside GP federation, has publicly questioned whether the SPA suits a rural area. Ellie Chandran proposes that Karen Lindqvist, the executive, writes to the practices instructing them to stop faxing, and that Dr Kapoor is left out of the design work because she opposes the project. Is this an appropriate way to lead the change, and why?
o: Yes, because the commissioner has made the SPA a contract condition, so the support of GP practices is not needed.
Yes, because a clear instruction from the executive saves time that would otherwise go on stakeholders who disagree.
No, because GP practices are independent organizations and so fall outside the project's stakeholders.
No, because Dr Kapoor is a key influencer whose concerns about rural access should be understood and addressed.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Stakeholder engagement identifies key influencers and builds relationships with them; resistance shows where engagement should be focused, and its causes should be explored rather than the stakeholder sidelined (see manual 3.2.2 and 3.4). Dr Kapoor can sway the Moorside practices, so understanding her concerns is central to adoption there.

n.0: A contract condition makes the SPA necessary but does not make GP practices use it; referrers' cooperation is needed for the benefits.
n.1: Sidelining people who disagree tends to deepen resistance; PRINCE2 7 asks the project to find out why they resist.
n.2: Stakeholders include anyone who can affect or be affected by the project, inside or outside the business; referring GP practices clearly are.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage. New rotas for the triage hub have been drafted. Lorraine Fenwick, the union representative for nursing staff, has asked to see them before they are agreed, and most nurses work shifts and join meetings online at lunchtime. Which action BEST applies the communication management approach?
o: Email the final rotas to all nursing staff and to the union once the project board has approved them.
Publish the draft rotas on the trust intranet and ask nurses to raise any concerns through their line managers.
Share the draft rotas with Lorraine Fenwick and hold online lunchtime sessions for nurses' feedback before they are agreed.
Present the draft rotas at the next board meeting and invite the union to raise concerns through formal consultation later.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: The communication management approach sets the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, each stakeholder group, as a controlled two-way flow (see manual 3.4). Sharing drafts with the union before agreement, and using the lunchtime online slot that staff can attend, gives the people affected a voice while it can still shape the rotas.

n.0: Sending rotas after approval is one-way and does not meet the union's request to see them before they are agreed.
n.1: Posting on the intranet is passive, and routing concerns through line managers gives no planned feedback channel to the project or the union.
n.3: Deferring the union's input until after the board has seen the rotas fails its request and limits two-way communication.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Ellie Chandran is drafting the communication management approach and has written this entry: 'Moorside GP practices: send referrals by fax to nurses they know; strongly influenced by Dr Kapoor; doubt that a single point of access suits a rural area; their cooperation will decide whether the Moorside roll-out succeeds.' Under which heading of the communication management approach should this entry be recorded, and why?
o: Communications schedule and procedures, because it sets out how the project will contact these practices.
Supporting tools and techniques, because it identifies fax as the channel that these practices currently use.
Resources, because it shows that extra staff effort will be needed to win over the Moorside practices.
Stakeholder analysis, because it records how this group is affected and how it could influence success.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is affected by the project and who can influence its success or failure, with their position and influencers (see manual 3.4). The entry describes the Moorside practices' interests, attitude and influence, so it belongs there; the schedule of messages to them would follow from it.

n.0: The entry sets out no message, channel or timing for contacting the practices; it analyses their interests and influence.
n.1: Supporting tools and techniques covers tools the project uses, such as communication platforms or analytics; fax is mentioned as the practices' current behaviour.
n.2: Resources covers the people and budget for communication activities; the entry says nothing about the effort the project will provide.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Greendale Ready Meals will not reduce its 150,000-meal minimum, and the latest consumer panel results suggest the two pan-fried recipes will sell far fewer meals than that in year one. Rob Hennessy, the executive, says there is no point reviewing the business case again: the £180,000 listing fee has already been paid and cannot be recovered, so the project must carry on as planned. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because stopping now would mean losing a listing fee that Harbridge's will not refund.
It applies it well, because the board has stated that the launch week in February cannot move.
It applies it poorly, because the justification must be revalidated against the remaining costs, risks and benefits.
It applies it poorly, because the business case should be confirmed through a benefits review before the trials stage.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Justification must remain valid and be revalidated throughout the project; if it is no longer justified, the project should be stopped (see manual 2.1). The listing fee is spent whichever way the board decides, so it cannot justify continuing. What matters is whether the costs still to come, including the Greendale minimum, and the risks are outweighed by the expected benefits. Rob is refusing to check the business case just as new information has emerged.

n.0: The fee is lost whether the project continues or stops, so it cannot justify the remaining investment; the principle looks forward at future costs, risks and benefits.
n.1: The fixed launch week is a constraint on the plan, not evidence that the project is still worth doing.
n.3: Benefits are confirmed mainly after closure; during the project the business case is maintained and checked at stage boundaries and when significant issues arise (manual 5.3.1).

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'starting up a project' process. One of the six recipes uses sesame, which has never been handled on the Fernhollow site. Nadia Osei asks Luke Barraclough to arrange visits to two other food manufacturers that have brought sesame onto their sites, reads the lessons reports from Fernhollow's last factory line upgrade, and records what she finds in the lessons log. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Learn from experience, because handling sesame is new to the business, so seeking lessons from other organizations matters more.
Focus on products, because the allergen controls found on the visits will become quality specifications for the sesame recipe.
Manage by exception, because the board has a very low appetite for allergen risk and wants early warning of any problem.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because Luke is responsible for allergen control and is building links with other firms.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Learn from experience: lessons are sought, recorded and acted on from the start, and when the work is a first for the business it is even more important to learn from others, including external organizations (see manual 2.2). Reviewing earlier lessons reports and recording findings in the lessons log is the 'assess previous lessons' activity of starting up a project (13.4.2).

n.1: The findings may later shape product descriptions, but the action described is gathering and recording lessons, not defining products or their quality specifications.
n.2: The low appetite explains why lessons matter here, but manage by exception is about setting tolerances and escalating forecast breaches; nothing here delegates authority or sets limits.
n.3: Luke is the means, not the purpose: the visits gather lessons rather than agree roles or build working relationships for the project.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Nadia Osei maps the people the project depends on who are not on the project board, including Tariq Javed at Harbridge's, Shona Mackintosh at Greendale and Jen Pascoe of the employee forum. She agrees with the board who will build and manage each relationship: Charlotte Vane will be the single contact for Tariq, and Dariusz Nowicki will meet Jen every fortnight. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by exception, because decisions about each stakeholder are being made at the most local level where the knowledge resides.
Focus on products, because the relationships are organized around the products that each stakeholder will receive or supply.
Ensure continued business justification, because the value of the Harbridge's listing depends on a good relationship with its buyer.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the team is agreeing who builds and maintains each key stakeholder relationship.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: The principle covers agreed roles and responsibilities, and it also requires the project management team to initiate and build relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (see manual 2.3). Mapping stakeholders outside the board and agreeing who will manage each relationship applies it directly.

n.0: Deciding at the most local level is about delegated decision-making within tolerances; agreeing who owns each stakeholder relationship is about roles and relationships.
n.1: The relationships are assigned to people according to their links with each stakeholder, not structured around product definitions or quality expectations.
n.2: The listing matters to the business case, but the action is about who manages relationships, not about checking whether the project remains desirable, viable and achievable.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Nadia Osei proposes that the concept and recipe stage should end before the order for the tray-sealing line is placed and before the Greendale supply agreement is signed. This lets the board see the final recipe choice and an updated business case before it commits to the line and to the 150,000-meal minimum. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because ending the stage there reduces the number of decisions the board must make in the development stage.
It applies it well, because the stage boundary gives the board a decision point before the largest commitments are made.
It applies it poorly, because the line order should be placed in initiation to protect the 14-week lead time and the launch week.
It applies it poorly, because stage boundaries should be set at equal intervals so that the board can plan its meetings.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Stages give the board review and decision points at which it assesses viability, and stage ends can be aligned with key decisions and external influences (see manual 2.4 and 7.2.3). Placing the boundary before the line purchase and the Greendale commitment means the board decides on those commitments with the recipe choice and an updated business case in front of it.

n.0: The boundary does not reduce the board's decisions; it places a decision point where it matters most.
n.2: Initiation plans the project; committing large sums to delivery before the board has authorized the project would undermine the controlled start that initiation provides.
n.3: Stage length should reflect decision points, risk and complexity, not a fixed calendar interval.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. With the business layer's agreement, the project plan sets no time tolerance on the launch week, a cost tolerance of plus or minus 5% of the £2.3 million budget, and a scope tolerance that allows the launch to go ahead with four of the six recipes. Nadia Osei will escalate if any of these is forecast to be exceeded. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by exception, because tolerances set the limits of the authority delegated to each management level.
Focus on products, because the scope tolerance defines which of the six recipes will be in the launch range.
Manage by stages, because tolerances are set for each stage so that the board can review them at stage ends.
Ensure continued business justification, because the cost tolerance protects the margin forecast in the business case.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Setting tolerances for the aspects of performance, and escalating when they are forecast to be exceeded, establishes the limits of delegated authority (see manual 2.5). Allowing as few as four recipes is a scope tolerance: the permitted range is manage by exception, even though the recipes themselves are defined under focus on products.

n.1: Defining the recipes and their requirements is focus on products; the permitted variation in how many are delivered is a tolerance.
n.2: These are project-level tolerances agreed with the business layer; stage-by-stage planning and decision points are a different principle.
n.3: The action sets limits of delegated authority for the plan; it does not review whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the concept and recipe stage. The consumer panel liked a dessert that one of the chefs made for a tasting, so Megan Cho asks two chefs to spend the next two-week cycle developing it as a seventh recipe. The project product description lists six ready meals, and Harbridge's has not asked for a dessert. How well does this apply the 'focus on products' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because co-creating products with the consumer panel improves their adoption by users.
It applies it well, because an extra recipe gives the launch a fallback if one of the six meals fails.
It applies it poorly, because chef time is going on a product that is outside the agreed scope of the project.
It applies it poorly, because a new recipe has to be approved by the Harbridge's buyer before work on it starts.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: A PRINCE2 project defines and delivers agreed products and does no more work than needed to deliver them, which controls scope creep (see manual 2.6). A seventh recipe is not in the project product description; if it is wanted, it should be raised as a request for change rather than worked on informally.

n.0: Co-creation with users is good practice for agreed products, but it does not justify spending effort on a product outside the agreed scope.
n.1: A dessert cannot stand in for a ready meal in a range of six meals, and any fallback should be agreed through the plan and change control, not created informally.
n.3: Harbridge's is a customer stakeholder, not the authority for the project's scope; changes to scope are decided through the project's own change control.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process. Nadia Osei proposes that the review notes Mint and Tallow produces at the end of each two-week cycle serve as its checkpoint reports, that highlight reports to the board take the form of a one-page dashboard, and that stage boundaries be called 'gate reviews', the term the directors already use for capital projects. The changes are recorded in the project initiation documentation. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
o: Yes, because the managing director signs off all investment over £250,000 and so can decide how the method is applied.
Yes, because reporting formats and terms are adapted to the delivery approach and the organization, and this is documented.
No, because checkpoint reports need to follow the standard PRINCE2 format so that work packages can be compared.
No, because replacing PRINCE2 terms with the organization's own terms weakens the method's common language.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Tailoring adapts processes, management products and terminology so that controls fit the project and the organization, and it must be documented and agreed, normally in the PID (see manual 2.7 and 15.4.1). Using the agency's cycle reviews as checkpoint reports, a lighter highlight format and the directors' own terms are all legitimate tailoring; the principles still apply in full.

n.0: Imogen Fairley's sign-off limit is a financial control in the business layer; tailoring is led by the project manager, documented in the PID and approved by the board.
n.2: Management products can be merged, renamed or given different formats; what matters is that they carry the information needed for control.
n.3: Terminology is one of the things PRINCE2 expects to be tailored, so that the method fits the organization's own language.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the concept and recipe stage. Mint and Tallow's designers work remotely, while Megan Cho's chefs are in the Fernhollow kitchen. At the last two tastings the pack designs did not reflect the recipes, and each side blamed the other. Nadia Osei arranges for the lead designers to join the chefs in the kitchen on every tasting day, with an informal lunch afterwards, and sets up a shared online board for work between tastings. Is this an appropriate approach to leading the team, and why?
o: Yes, because a hybrid team needs deliberate ways to build social cohesion and trust across the silos.
Yes, because the senior supplier is accountable for the quality of the products that suppliers deliver.
No, because the agency is a contracted supplier, so its people are managed by its own team manager.
No, because team-building activities are a matter for each organization's line managers, not the project.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Virtual, remote and hybrid teams do not share information organically; they need deliberate methods, such as synchronized co-location days for key people, to build social cohesion and trust across project silos (see manual 3.3.3). Bringing designers and chefs together on tasting days, with a shared board in between, focuses on the relationship that is failing.

n.1: It is true that the senior supplier is accountable for supplier quality, but that does not explain why bringing the two groups together is the right response.
n.2: The agency's team manager directs its own team's work, but building cohesion across the wider project ecosystem is part of leading the project team.
n.3: Leading and building the temporary project team, including across organizational boundaries, is part of the project manager's role.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the concept and recipe stage. None of Megan Cho's four chefs has worked with sesame or under strict allergen segregation. To save time, Dariusz Nowicki suggests that the chefs start trial batches of the sesame recipe next week and that Luke Barraclough's team tests the batches afterwards for cross-contact. Is this an appropriate approach to managing the team, and why?
o: Yes, because quality control by a team independent of production gives the board confidence in the results.
Yes, because the chefs' training is a line management matter that sits outside the project manager's remit.
No, because the board's very low appetite for allergen risk means the sesame recipe should be dropped.
No, because the chefs lack a competence the work needs, and the gap should be closed by training or reassigning work.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Building an effective team includes understanding the competencies people need, identifying gaps and mitigating them, for example by upskilling or by shifting responsibilities to more suitable people (see manual 3.3.2). A clear competency gap has been found in a high-risk area, and testing the batches afterwards does not close it.

n.0: Independent testing is quality control of the output; it does not give the chefs the competence they lack before they start handling sesame.
n.1: Some motivators such as pay sit outside the project manager's remit, but identifying and closing the competency gaps that project work depends on is part of building the team.
n.2: Dropping a recipe would be a scope decision for the board; a low appetite calls for strong allergen controls and competent people, not removal of the recipe by default.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Night shift operators have stopped volunteering for training on the new tray-sealing line, and rumours are spreading that it will cut jobs. Dariusz Nowicki wants to tell them that the line is going in whatever they think. Instead, Nadia Osei and Dariusz meet Jen Pascoe, who represents the operators on the employee forum, to find out what lies behind the resistance before deciding how to respond. Is this an appropriate approach to leading change, and why?
o: Yes, because Jen Pascoe's views must be recorded in the issue register as a concern before any action is taken.
Yes, because resistance should be investigated to understand its causes, working with key influencers such as Jen.
No, because Jen holds no role in the project management team, so engagement should go through the senior user.
No, because the line has been ordered and the change will happen, so the priority is to announce the decision clearly.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Pockets of resistance show where communication and engagement should focus: the project should find out why stakeholders resist rather than sideline them, and identify key influencers, who may hold no formal role (see manual 3.2.2 and 3.4). Jen influences the night shift, so working with her to understand the concerns is the right first step.

n.0: A concern could be logged, but logging it is not what makes the approach appropriate; the value lies in understanding the resistance through a key influencer.
n.2: Projects must involve key people who are critical to success even if they hold no formal role, and Jen is such a person.
n.3: Announcing the decision without understanding the resistance risks deepening it; the change still needs the operators' support to work.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the trials stage. After launch the range will be run by the normal operations team, and every production run of the sesame recipe will need a full allergen clean-down that the operators have never carried out. Nadia Osei wants to move the factory from its current ways of working to this target state. Which action is MOST LIKELY to achieve this?
o: Issue detailed written clean-down procedures to every operator a week before the first production run.
Ask Luke Barraclough to audit operators after launch and record each failure in the issue register.
Have Dariusz Nowicki announce the new shift routines at the employee forum once the line is commissioned.
Involve the operators and Jen Pascoe in designing and testing the clean-down routines during the trials.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Co-creation involves users and key influencers in designing products and ways of working so that they are adopted by the organization (see manual 3.3). Enabling activities before and during transition, such as trials and training, help move people from the current state to the target state (3.2.1). Designing the routines with the operators during trials builds understanding and ownership before launch.

n.0: Written procedures issued late, without involvement, do not build the understanding or commitment that a new way of working needs.
n.1: Auditing after launch finds failures once the transition has happened; it does not prepare people for the target state.
n.2: Announcing routines after they are fixed tells people what will change but does not involve them in shaping it.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the development stage. Charlotte Vane has already told Tariq Javed, the Harbridge's buyer, that all six recipes will launch. Two recipes are now at risk, and Tariq has heard rumours from the packaging supplier. The communication management approach names Charlotte as Tariq's single contact, with a call every fortnight. Which action BEST applies the communication management approach?
o: Send Tariq the project's highlight reports so that he sees the same information as the project board.
Wait until the factory trials are complete so that Tariq is given a firm list of recipes at one time.
Have Charlotte use the next fortnightly call to give Tariq an honest view of readiness and invite his questions.
Ask Megan Cho to call the Harbridge's technical team directly to explain the problems with the two recipes.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: The communication management approach sets the means and frequency of communication with, and feedback from, each stakeholder, giving a controlled two-way flow that avoids misconceptions (see manual 3.4). Using the agreed channel and contact, with an honest message and a chance for Tariq to respond, follows the approach and deals with the rumours.

n.0: Highlight reports are written for the project board; sending internal reports to a customer is not the agreed channel and may share sensitive information.
n.1: Delaying lets the rumours shape Tariq's view; the approach relies on regular two-way communication, not silence until there is certainty.
n.3: Bypassing the agreed single contact risks mixed messages to a key customer; Charlotte owns the relationship.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in the 'initiating a project' process, and Nadia Osei is drafting the communication management approach. She notes that the night shift operators will be affected both by the three-week shutdown and by the new line, and that Jen Pascoe, through the employee forum, has strong influence over whether they support the change. Under which heading of the communication management approach should this be recorded?
o: Communications schedule and procedures
Stakeholder analysis
Supporting tools and techniques
Resources
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Stakeholder analysis identifies who is affected by the outcome or by the way the project is delivered, and who can influence its success or failure (communication management approach, see manual 3.4). The operators' exposure and Jen's influence belong there.

n.0: The schedule and procedures set out how, when and through which channels each group is communicated with; this entry identifies who is affected and who has influence.
n.2: Supporting tools and techniques covers platforms and tools such as communications or analytics software.
n.3: Resources covers the people and budget needed to carry out communication activities, not the analysis of stakeholders.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Cllr Yvonne Price has announced the race in the local media. She tells Kezia Oduya that, because the cabinet is committed and the date is fixed with the national athletics body, the business case needs to be written once to secure authorization and will not need updating at stage boundaries. How well does this apply the 'ensure continued business justification' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because political commitment and a fixed date are valid reasons for the project and belong in the business case.
It applies it well, because the executive, not the project manager, decides how often the business case is reviewed.
It applies it poorly, because the justification must stay valid throughout, so the business case is updated and checked each stage.
It applies it poorly, because the cabinet member should own the business case as the event's public champion.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: The justification must remain valid and be revalidated throughout the project; if it is lost, the project should be changed or stopped (see manual 2.1). The project manager maintains the business case at each stage end and the board checks it before authorizing the next stage (5.3.1). Entries, sponsorship and costs against the £300,000 cap can all change, so a one-off business case applies the principle poorly.

n.0: Commitment and the fixed date explain why the project was started; they do not remove the need to revalidate the justification as costs, entries and sponsorship change.
n.1: The executive is accountable for the business case, but the principle requires it to be maintained and checked throughout; no role can decide to stop revalidating it.
n.3: The executive owns the business case (Andrew Mallory holds the budget); in any case the weakness here is that the case would not be revalidated, not who owns it.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'starting up a project' process. The council has never run an event of this size. Kezia Oduya arranges calls with the organizers of two established half marathons in other cities, reads the independent review of the collapse at Paceline's 10k race, and records what she learns in the lessons log. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Learn from experience, because the event is a first for the council, so seeking lessons from outside organizations matters even more.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the review concerns how Paceline carried out its medical role at the 10k.
Ensure continued business justification, because other cities' experience shows whether a half marathon brings in enough local spending.
Manage by exception, because the lessons will help Kezia decide which problems she can deal with herself and which to escalate.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Learn from experience: lessons are sought, recorded and acted on from the start, and when a project is a first for the organization it is even more important to learn from others, including outside organizations (see manual 2.2). Reviewing earlier reports and consulting people with experience of similar projects is the 'assess previous lessons' activity, recorded in the lessons log (13.4.2).

n.1: The review is one of the sources of lessons; Kezia is gathering and recording lessons, not agreeing roles or building relationships.
n.2: Kezia is not checking whether this project is still desirable, viable and achievable; she is collecting experience from other events.
n.3: Manage by exception is about tolerances and escalation; nothing here sets limits of delegated authority.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kezia Oduya sets up a monthly liaison group with Inspector Ravi Sandhu of the safety advisory group, Colin Mayfield of the traders' association, Rev Judith Akers and a residents' representative. She agrees with each of them who their contact in the project team is and what they can expect to hear, and when. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Learn from experience, because the liaison group will collect lessons from people who have lived through earlier road closures.
Tailor to suit the project, because a liaison group adapts the method to the council's usual way of working with communities.
Manage by stages, because the group will meet at fixed intervals that give the board regular points to review the project.
Define roles, responsibilities and relationships, because the team is building relationships with external stakeholders.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: The principle covers agreed roles and responsibilities and also the project management team initiating and building relationships with and between internal and external stakeholders (see manual 2.3). Kezia is setting up a relationship with each external group and agreeing what each can expect from the project.

n.0: The group may surface useful experience, but its purpose here is to build and manage relationships, not to gather lessons.
n.1: Tailoring adapts processes, products, roles or terms to the project; setting up stakeholder relationships is not a tailoring decision.
n.2: Manage by stages concerns stage-by-stage planning and board decision points; a monthly liaison group is not a stage boundary.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The draft plan has a 16-week build-up stage. Kezia Oduya proposes splitting it into two stages, with a boundary straight after the safety advisory group's decision eight weeks before race day, so that the board decides whether to commit the largest infrastructure spending once it knows the event can go ahead. How well does this apply the 'manage by stages' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because shorter stages let the board set tighter tolerances for Kezia to work within.
It applies it well, because stage boundaries are decision points and can be aligned with key external events.
It applies it poorly, because adding a stage increases the time that senior managers spend directing the project.
It applies it poorly, because the number of stages was settled when the board authorized initiation.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Stages give the board review and decision points at which it assesses viability, and stage ends can be aligned with external influences (see manual 2.4). Without the safety advisory group's approval the event cannot go ahead, so a boundary after that decision lets the board commit the largest spending at the right moment.

n.0: Setting tolerances is manage by exception; the reason for this boundary is to create a decision point around the approval.
n.2: It is true that more stages add to the board's burden, but with a go or no-go approval and a low appetite for safety risk, more control here is justified.
n.3: Stages are decided as the project plan is prepared in initiation; the brief and initiation stage plan approved earlier do not fix them.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage, which has a cost tolerance of plus or minus £15,000. The barrier hire contract comes in £8,000 above the stage plan. Kezia Oduya finds a matching saving in printing costs, adjusts the stage plan and reports both changes in her next highlight report, without asking the board for a decision. Which principle is being applied, and why?
o: Manage by stages, because the board will review the changed costs when it next authorizes a stage.
Ensure continued business justification, because keeping to the cost plan protects the council's £300,000 cap.
Manage by exception, because the forecast stays within the stage tolerance that the board delegated to Kezia.
Focus on products, because the barriers are a product whose cost is set in their product description.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Manage by exception sets limits of delegated authority through tolerances; while the stage is forecast to stay within tolerance the project manager can adjust without escalating, and the board is kept informed through highlight reports (see manual 2.5 and 11.2.6).

n.0: The board does review costs at stage ends, but Kezia's freedom to act now comes from the tolerance delegated to her, not from the next stage boundary.
n.1: Protecting the cap matters, but the action shows a decision taken within delegated limits rather than a check of whether the project is still worth doing.
n.3: A product description sets a product's purpose and quality, not its cost; the decision rests on the stage cost tolerance.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kezia Oduya's draft plan for the build-up stage is a list of tasks such as 'sort volunteers', 'do marketing' and 'meetings with Paceline', each with a duration and an owner. Andrew Mallory likes it because the events team plans its markets this way. Nothing describes what each piece of work must produce or the standard it must meet. How well does this apply the 'focus on products' principle, and why?
o: It applies it well, because a simple task list is a reasonable way of tailoring the method for an in-house events team.
It applies it well, because each task has a named owner, which makes clear who is responsible for the work.
It applies it poorly, because the plan should be reviewed by the safety advisory group before the build-up stage starts.
It applies it poorly, because the plan is task-based and does not define the products and the quality they must meet.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: The principle requires the project to be output-oriented: products are defined, with their quality expectations, in product descriptions, and these drive planning, quality and scope control (see manual 2.6). A list of tasks with no defined outputs is work-oriented and leaves scope and standards unclear.

n.0: Tailoring can simplify products and formats, but it cannot remove a principle; the plan still needs defined products.
n.1: Named owners clarify who does the work, but they do not define what must be delivered or to what standard.
n.2: The safety advisory group approves the event safety plan, not the project's stage plans; this does not explain the weakness.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the 'initiating a project' process. Kezia Oduya proposes that highlight reports be a two-page summary every four weeks in the planning and approvals stage, then every two weeks in the build-up stage and daily during event week, when the pace and the safety risks are highest. The board would review them online instead of meeting. Is this an appropriate application of the 'tailor to suit the project' principle, and why?
o: Yes, because frequent highlight reports keep Cllr Yvonne Price ready for questions from the local media.
Yes, because the frequency and formality of reporting are matched to the pace and risk of each stage.
No, because the reporting frequency should stay the same in every stage once the board has set it.
No, because tailoring decisions are approved by the business layer rather than by the project board.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Tailoring makes project controls fit the project's scale, complexity, importance and risk, for example the frequency and formality of reports and reviews (see manual 2.7). Reporting more often as risk rises, and letting a busy board review online, is proportionate tailoring recorded in the PID.

n.0: Highlight reports are for the project board; media briefings are planned through the communication management approach, so this is not a tailoring reason.
n.2: Reporting frequency can be varied to suit the control needed at different points in the project.
n.3: Tailoring is documented in the PID, which the project board approves when it authorizes the project.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the planning and approvals stage. Paceline's operations team works from its head office in another city, and the council's events officers contact them mainly by email. Misunderstandings about road closure times have twice caused rework. Kezia Oduya arranges a joint planning day every fortnight on the riverside, where Lisa Ventnor's team and the events officers walk parts of the course together and agree actions. Is this an appropriate way to manage the project team, and why?
o: Yes, because working side by side lets Kezia direct Paceline's staff without going through Lisa Ventnor.
Yes, because regular, purposeful meetings build trust and social cohesion between teams from different organizations.
No, because Paceline's staff are accountable to Greg Halloran, so their ways of working are a matter for Paceline.
No, because joint team building should wait until the build-up stage, when the volunteers join the project.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Bringing teams together means building social cohesion through people meeting purposefully and regularly, creating trust across silos; teams that are not co-located need deliberate methods such as planned joint days (see manual 3.3.3). Here two organizations' teams are misunderstanding each other by email.

n.0: Kezia should work through the team manager; the value of the days is shared understanding, not bypassing Lisa.
n.2: Greg Halloran commits Paceline's staff, but the problem lies between the two teams, which the project manager should help to work together.
n.3: Delaying would let the rework continue; cohesion is needed now between the teams already working together.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the build-up stage. The events officer booking grandstands, barriers and toilets has booked equipment only for park concerts before. Two bookings have been late and one supplier delivered the wrong barriers. Lisa Ventnor's logistics team at Paceline has made bookings of this kind for many races. Which action is MOST appropriate for Kezia Oduya to take?
o: Pair the officer with Paceline's logistics team for the remaining bookings, arrange training and review progress at each checkpoint.
Ask Andrew Mallory, as executive, to approve each booking personally so that mistakes are caught before orders are placed.
Record the late bookings in the lessons log for future events and leave the work with the officer until race day.
Widen the officer's work package tolerances so that late bookings no longer need to be reported to her.
Practitioner: Principles & People.w: Building effective teams means understanding people's capabilities, identifying competency gaps and mitigating them, for example by upskilling or shifting responsibilities to more suitable people (see manual 3.3.2). Pairing the officer with experienced Paceline staff and arranging training closes the gap while keeping the work moving.

n.1: The executive directs the project and does not manage day-to-day bookings; this adds a bottleneck without closing the gap.
n.2: Recording a lesson is useful, but leaving the gap unaddressed risks more errors before race day.
n.3: Widening tolerances hides the problem from the project manager rather than dealing with the capability gap.

Practitioner: Principles & People.q: The Carrowford Half Marathon project is in the planning and approvals stage.
