No, because an option that would leave the Leeds systems with no site to run in is not viable and should be dropped.
No, because the options should be limited to cloud providers, as the society's board has approved the cloud strategy.
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: When developing the business case, the basic options are do nothing differently, do the minimum and do more than the minimum. Do nothing differently is always considered first because it is the baseline for quantifying the other options; the difference between them is what the investment buys (see manual 5.3.1).

n.0: Justification is about value, weighing benefits against costs and risks; the cheapest option is not necessarily the best value.
n.2: Even when doing nothing differently is not viable, it is still the baseline against which the costs and benefits of the other options are measured, so it is not dropped.
n.3: Even where the direction is set, the chosen option must be justified as the best value against the alternatives.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. Mairi Campbell drafts the benefits management approach. It sets out how the £1.4 million running cost saving and the four-hour recovery time will be measured, schedules reviews in years two and three after closure, and names Mairi as the person who will measure and report these benefits after the project has closed. Is this an effective way to apply the business case practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager prepares the benefits management approach on behalf of the executive.
Yes, because carrying out post-project benefits reviews is one of the activities in closing a project.
No, because benefits should be measured at each stage boundary rather than after the project has closed.
No, because the senior user is responsible for showing that benefits are on track, including after closure.
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: The senior user is responsible for specifying benefits, for demonstrating that forecast benefits are on track and for the continued realization of benefits after the project closes (see manual 6.2.4.2); post-project benefits reviews are carried out by the business, not by the project (see manual 5.3.1, 'confirm'). Mairi's project manager role ends at closure, so she cannot own the later measurement.

n.0: It is true that the project manager prepares the approach, but that does not make her the right person to measure benefits after her role has ended.
n.1: Closing a project plans the post-project benefits reviews; carrying them out is done by the business after closure.
n.2: Benefits are checked at stage boundaries, but the main savings arrive from year three, after closure, so post-project reviews are still needed.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Matching set (organizing). The project board for Project Skyline is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual is the most appropriate for each role? Statement 1 of 3: Executive.
o: Fraser McIntyre
Aileen Docherty
Joanne Pettigrew
Lena Fischer
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: The executive is the single point of accountability who owns the business case and secures funding. Fraser McIntyre received the mandate, holds the IT and operations budget and sits on the executive committee (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.1: Aileen Docherty reports to Fraser McIntyre and is not the budget holder; she also wants to widen the scope, which makes her a poor choice to own the business case.
n.2: Joanne Pettigrew's teams use the applications, which suits the user interest rather than accountability for the investment.
n.3: Lena Fischer works for the supplier; the executive represents the business interest of Brennan Mutual.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Matching set (organizing). The project board for Project Skyline is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual is the most appropriate for each role? Statement 2 of 3: Senior user.
o: Fraser McIntyre
Aileen Docherty
Joanne Pettigrew
Lena Fischer
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: The senior user represents those who will use the products, specifies user requirements and benefits and commits user resources. Joanne Pettigrew runs the branches and contact centre, whose teams use most of the applications being migrated (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.0: Fraser McIntyre holds the budget and the mandate, which suits the executive role.
n.1: Aileen Docherty leads the IT function, which provides services rather than using the member-facing applications.
n.3: Lena Fischer represents Stratoshift, a supplier, not the people who will use the migrated applications.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Matching set (organizing). The project board for Project Skyline is being appointed. Using the additional information about the people, which individual is the most appropriate for each role? Statement 3 of 3: Senior supplier representing the cloud partner.
o: Fraser McIntyre
Aileen Docherty
Joanne Pettigrew
Lena Fischer
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: The senior supplier commits supplier people and resources and is accountable for the quality of the products the supplier delivers. Lena Fischer is Stratoshift's engagement director, who commits its people and is accountable for the quality of its work (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B).

n.0: Fraser McIntyre represents the business interest as executive, not the cloud partner.
n.1: Aileen Docherty is the society's own chief information officer; she cannot commit Stratoshift's people or answer for the quality of its work.
n.2: Joanne Pettigrew represents the users of the applications, not the supplier.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. Using the work breakdown structure, Mairi Campbell and Nicola Graham decide that Stratoshift will deliver the landing zone and the application migrations, the core banking vendor will move its own system, and the society's IT operations team will carry out decommissioning. They record this in the commercial management approach and plan the team structure around it. Which step of the organizational design and development technique is being applied, and why?
o: Understand the organizational ecosystem, because it identifies the society's existing structures and governance.
Design the project ecosystem, because it decides how work and people are organized, using the WBS and delivery model.
Develop the project ecosystem, because it builds the skills and relationships of the people joining the project.
Manage ongoing changes to the project ecosystem, because suppliers will join and leave as the stages progress.
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: Designing the project ecosystem decides how the work and people will be organized; it is shaped by the work breakdown structure and the commercial management approach, including the delivery model that shows which parts external suppliers deliver (see manual 6.3.1).

n.0: Understanding the organizational ecosystem looks at the existing structures, governance and policies; here the team is deciding who will deliver which parts of the work.
n.2: Developing the ecosystem covers onboarding, skills assessment and culture once people join; the allocation of work comes first.
n.3: Managing ongoing changes deals with changing needs over the lifecycle; this is the initial design of who does what.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. To save money, Mairi Campbell proposes that the project support officer from the change team, who maintains the project's registers, also carries out business assurance for each migration wave and reports the findings to Fraser McIntyre. Victoria Sharma has asked for independent assurance of every wave. Is this an effective way to apply the organizing practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project board decides how project assurance is carried out and who carries it out.
Yes, because the project support officer already holds the data that business assurance needs to review.
No, because project assurance must be independent of the project manager and kept separate from project support.
No, because project assurance for a regulated firm should be carried out by internal audit rather than by staff.
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: Project assurance is the board's responsibility and must be independent of the project manager; it cannot be given to the project manager, team members or project support, and support must be kept separate from assurance (see manual 6.2.4 and appendix B). A support officer working for Mairi cannot give the independent assurance required.

n.0: The board does decide how assurance is done, but within the rule that assurance cannot be assigned to project support.
n.1: Access to the data does not provide independence; the person maintaining the registers would be checking their own work.
n.3: Assurance can be carried out by board members, people appointed from the business or external parties; it does not have to be internal audit.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Matching set (plans). Which role should carry out each of these planning actions on Project Skyline? Statement 1 of 3: Set the cost tolerance of plus or minus 7.5% for the project and document it in the project mandate.
o: Business layer
Executive
Project manager
Team manager
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: The business layer provides the planning standards and sets the project tolerances, documenting them in the project mandate (see manual chapter 7, table 7.1).

n.1: The executive defines tolerances for each stage; project-level tolerances are set by the business layer above the board.
n.2: The project manager sets work package tolerances and works within stage tolerances; project tolerances come from the business layer.
n.3: The team manager works within work package tolerances and has no part in setting project tolerances.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Matching set (plans). Which role should carry out each of these planning actions on Project Skyline? Statement 2 of 3: Prepare the schedule for the wave 2 migration work package.
o: Business layer
Executive
Project manager
Team manager
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: The team manager prepares the schedule for each work package, and a team plan where needed (see manual chapter 7, table 7.1). On Project Skyline this would be Arjun Menon for the Stratoshift migration work.

n.0: The business layer sets standards and project tolerances; it does not schedule work packages.
n.1: The executive sets stage tolerances and approves stage plans, not the schedules for individual work packages.
n.2: The project manager prepares the stage plan and work package descriptions; the detailed schedule for a work package is the team manager's.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Matching set (plans). Which role should carry out each of these planning actions on Project Skyline? Statement 3 of 3: Define the time and cost tolerances for the wave migration stage and approve its stage plan.
o: Business layer
Executive
Project manager
Team manager
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: The executive defines the tolerances for each stage and approves the stage plans (see manual chapter 7, table 7.1).

n.0: The business layer sets project tolerances; stage tolerances are set on the project board side by the executive.
n.2: The project manager prepares the stage plan but cannot approve it or set the tolerances that limit his or her own authority.
n.3: The team manager works within work package tolerances and does not approve stage plans.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. Mairi Campbell and Steven Clarke create a product breakdown structure for the project plan and then draw a product flow diagram. It shows that wave 2 needs the shared network product from wave 1, and that the core banking move depends on the vendor's hosted service, which the vendor will provide under its own contract. Is this an appropriate application of the plans technique, and why?
o: Yes, because the product flow diagram shows the sequence of products and their dependencies, including external ones.
Yes, because a product flow diagram replaces the need to prepare a schedule for the project plan.
No, because products supplied under a separate contract are outside the project's control and should be left out.
No, because product breakdown structures are prepared for stage plans rather than for the project plan.
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: In product-based planning the product breakdown structure is followed by a product flow diagram showing the sequence in which products are produced and the dependencies between them, including external products the project relies on (see manual 7.3.1).

n.1: The product flow diagram feeds the later planning steps; preparing the schedule is still a separate step of the technique.
n.2: External products are shown precisely because the project depends on them; this makes the external dependency visible and manageable.
n.3: Products are defined and analysed for every level of plan, including the project plan.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Project Skyline is in the 'initiating a project' process. Mairi Campbell prepares a day-by-day plan for every application in all three migration waves, covering the next 14 months, and tells the board that no further stage plans will be needed. The pilot wave, which will show how long migrations really take, has not yet run. Is this an effective way to apply the plans practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a detailed plan made now lets the board set the tolerances for every later stage at once.
Yes, because a linear-sequential approach needs every product and task to be planned in detail before work starts.
No, because the stage plan for the wave migration stage should be prepared by Arjun Menon as team manager.
No, because each stage plan should be prepared near the end of the previous stage, within the planning horizon.
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: Only the near future can be planned in detail, so PRINCE2 uses a high-level project plan plus a detailed stage plan for the current stage; each later stage plan is prepared near the end of the stage before it, when results such as the pilot wave are known (see manual 7.2.1 and 7.2.2.2).

n.0: Stage tolerances are set when each stage plan is approved; setting them all now on untested estimates weakens control.
n.1: Linear-sequential delivery defines products in detail early, but stage plans are still prepared near the end of the previous stage.
n.2: Stage plans are prepared by the project manager; team managers prepare team plans and work package schedules.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Matching set (quality). Mairi Campbell and Steven Clarke are writing the product description for a 'migrated application', to be used for every wave. Which heading of the product description should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Allows a member or staff application to run in the cloud landing zone so that the society can close its data centres.
o: Purpose
Composition
Derivation
Quality specifications
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: The purpose heading explains what the product is for and why it is needed (product description composition, manual chapter 8). Here it lets each application run in the cloud so that the data centres can close.

n.1: Composition lists the parts that make up the product, not why the product is needed.
n.2: Derivation states what the product is developed from, not what it is for.
n.3: Quality specifications set out measurable characteristics the product must meet; this statement explains why the product exists.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Matching set (quality). Mairi Campbell and Steven Clarke are writing the product description for a 'migrated application', to be used for every wave. Which heading of the product description should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: The application running in the landing zone, its operating procedures for the new environment and its rollback procedure.
o: Purpose
Composition
Derivation
Quality specifications
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: Composition lists the parts that make up the product (product description composition, manual chapter 8): the running application, its operating procedures and its rollback procedure.

n.0: The statement lists the product's parts; it does not explain what the product is for.
n.2: Derivation identifies what the product comes from, such as the existing application; these are the parts of the finished product.
n.3: Quality specifications would state the measures each part must meet, such as passing resilience tests; this statement lists the parts.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Matching set (quality). Mairi Campbell and Steven Clarke are writing the product description for a 'migrated application', to be used for every wave. Which heading of the product description should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: The existing application and its configuration in the Falkirk or Leeds data centre, and the target cloud architecture designed by Steven Clarke.
o: Purpose
Composition
Derivation
Quality specifications
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: Derivation states where the product comes from, that is the source products it is developed from (product description composition, manual chapter 8): the existing application and its configuration, plus the target architecture.

n.0: The statement describes source material, not why the product is needed.
n.1: These are inputs to the product rather than the parts of the finished migrated application.
n.3: No measurable quality criteria are stated; these are the products it is derived from.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Project Skyline is in the wave migration stage. Callum Reid's internal audit team, which reports to the audit committee and not to the project, reviews whether the project's testing of migrated applications meets the standards in the society's quality management system. Which element of quality management is this, and why?
o: Project assurance, because it gives the project board confidence that the project is being run correctly.
Quality assurance, because it is carried out independently of the project management team by a business function.
Quality control, because it checks whether the migrated applications meet their quality specifications.
Quality planning, because it confirms the standards that the quality management approach should refer to.
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: Quality assurance is a planned, systematic activity, carried out independently of the project management team, typically by a business function, that checks the project's quality control arrangements are appropriate (see manual 8.2.3). Internal audit reports to the audit committee, not to the project board.

n.0: Project assurance is the project board's responsibility, independent of the project manager but part of the project; internal audit here works for the audit committee, outside the project.
n.2: Quality control tests the products themselves; internal audit is reviewing whether the testing arrangements are adequate.
n.3: Quality planning produces the quality management approach and product descriptions; this review takes place during delivery.

Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.q: Project Skyline is in the wave migration stage. The product description for a migrated application requires a tested rollback for every application before switch-over. To keep wave 2 on schedule, Arjun Menon suggests testing the rollback for one application of each type and assuming that the rest will work. Mairi Campbell agrees without consulting anyone else. How well does this apply the quality practice, and why?
o: It applies it well, because the team manager decides which quality methods are used for the products in a work package.
It applies it well, because testing one application of each type gives the board enough confidence in the wave.
It applies it poorly, because each product should be checked against its quality specifications, and changing them needs approval.
It applies it poorly, because rollback testing should be carried out by internal audit as the quality assurance function.
Practitioner: Business Case to Quality.w: Quality control checks each product against the quality specifications in its product description, and results are recorded in the quality register. The product description is part of the baseline, so relaxing a specification is a change that goes through issue and change control, not an informal agreement (see manual 8.2.2; change control is part of the issues practice, ch 10).

n.0: Quality methods are set in the product descriptions and the quality management approach; a team manager cannot drop a required test.
n.1: The specification requires a tested rollback for every application, reflecting the board's very low appetite for outages; sampling does not meet it.
n.3: Testing products is quality control by the project; internal audit provides quality assurance by reviewing whether those controls are adequate.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (risk). Hannah Okoro is entering a new risk about the council tax integration in the risk register for Permits Online. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 1 of 3: Because the ICT team is supporting three other projects, the council tax integration may be finished late, which would delay the start of the private beta.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: A risk description sets out the cause (the ICT team's other commitments), the uncertain event (late integration) and the effect on objectives (a delayed private beta) (see manual 9.2.1 and 9.5).

n.0: No person is named; the statement describes what the risk is.
n.2: No timing is given for when the risk might occur.
n.3: No action or person carrying it out is named; this is the cause, event and effect.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (risk). Hannah Okoro is entering a new risk about the council tax integration in the risk register for Permits Online. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 2 of 3: The risk could occur in weeks 6 to 10 of the discovery and alpha stage, when the integration is due to be built.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Proximity records how close in time the risk is likely to occur (see manual 9.5).

n.0: No person is named; this states when the risk might occur.
n.1: This states when the risk might occur, not its cause, event and effect.
n.3: No agreed action or person carrying it out is named.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (risk). Hannah Okoro is entering a new risk about the council tax integration in the risk register for Permits Online. Which heading of the risk register should each piece of information be recorded under? Statement 3 of 3: Alan Briggs, ICT infrastructure manager, is responsible for managing this risk and its response.
o: Risk owner
Risk description
Proximity
Risk action owner
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The risk owner is the person assigned to take responsibility for managing a risk and responding to it; a risk action owner carries out specific agreed actions on the owner's behalf (see manual 9.2 and the risk register composition).

n.1: This names who manages the risk, not what the risk is.
n.2: No timing is given for when the risk might occur.
n.3: A risk action owner carries out a specific agreed action for the risk owner; Alan Briggs is responsible for managing the risk as a whole.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (issues). The PMO's second officer provides project support for Permits Online, and Tom Achebe is the team manager for the build. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 1 of 3: Enter a new request for change from the Old Town Residents' Association in the issue register.
o: Senior user
Project manager
Team manager
Project support
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Project support administers the issue and change control procedures by maintaining the issue register (issues roles, manual table 10.2).

n.0: The senior user decides on escalated issues; keeping the register is administration.
n.1: The project manager runs the issue procedure and keeps the register when there is no project support; here project support is in place.
n.2: Team managers implement corrective actions in their work packages; they do not keep the issue register.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (issues). The PMO's second officer provides project support for Permits Online, and Tom Achebe is the team manager for the build. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 2 of 3: Carry out the agreed rework of the payment page within the team's current work package after it failed an accessibility check.
o: Senior user
Project manager
Team manager
Project support
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Team managers implement corrective actions within their work packages (issues roles, manual table 10.2).

n.0: The senior user decides on escalated issues; the rework itself is done by the team.
n.1: The project manager authorizes corrective action and creates new work packages where needed, but carrying out rework within the current work package falls to the team manager.
n.3: Project support administers the issue register; it does not rework products.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (issues). The PMO's second officer provides project support for Permits Online, and Tom Achebe is the team manager for the build. Which role should carry out each action? Statement 3 of 3: Decide on an escalated request for change, with a focus on protecting the expected cut in processing time.
o: Senior user
Project manager
Team manager
Project support
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: When issues are escalated, the senior user makes decisions with a focus on safeguarding the expected benefits (issues roles, manual table 10.2).

n.1: The project manager handles issues within delegated authority; an escalated request is decided above that level, where the senior user protects the expected benefits.
n.2: Team managers implement actions; they do not decide escalated issues.
n.3: Project support records the decision in the issue register; it does not make it.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (progress). Permits Online is in the private beta stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: Tom Achebe tells Hannah Okoro, at the interval set in his work package, what his team completed in the last sprint and what is planned next.
o: Checkpoint report
Highlight report
Exception report
Daily log
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: A checkpoint report is produced by the team manager for the project manager on the status of a work package, at the frequency set in the work package (see manual 11.5).

n.1: Highlight reports go from the project manager to the board on the status of the stage.
n.2: Nothing is forecast to exceed tolerance.
n.3: This is formal work package reporting from a team manager, not an informal note.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (progress). Permits Online is in the private beta stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: Hannah Okoro notes that Fiona McRae mentioned in confidence that two permit officers are thinking of retiring early, and that she will follow it up.
o: Checkpoint report
Highlight report
Exception report
Daily log
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The daily log is the project manager's informal record of issues, actions and observations, including sensitive matters that would not suit open records (see manual 11.5).

n.0: This is not work package status from a team manager.
n.1: A sensitive, informal matter shared in confidence does not belong in a report to the board.
n.2: No tolerance breach is forecast.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (progress). Permits Online is in the private beta stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: Hannah Okoro tells the board that the integration delay is now forecast to exceed the stage time tolerance, and sets out options and a recommendation.
o: Checkpoint report
Highlight report
Exception report
Daily log
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: An exception report is produced by the project manager when a stage plan is forecast to exceed its tolerances, giving the options and a recommendation (see manual 11.3.1).

n.0: Checkpoint reports go from the team manager to the project manager.
n.1: A highlight report gives routine stage status; a forecast breach of stage tolerance calls for an exception report.
n.3: A forecast tolerance breach must be escalated formally, not noted informally.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Permits Online has a risk that the independent accessibility audit could find failures shortly before go-live, delaying the launch past 31 October. Hannah Okoro agrees with Tom Achebe that automated accessibility checks and testing with assistive technology users will run in every sprint, and that an interim audit will take place at the end of the private beta. Which type of risk response is this, and why?
o: Avoid, because the extra testing removes any chance that the final audit will find accessibility failures.
Reduce, because action taken now lowers the chance and impact of audit failures, though some risk remains.
Transfer, because Kestrel Lane will carry out the testing and so takes on the impact under its contract.
Prepare contingent plans, because the interim audit will be used if failures are found late in the project.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: A reduce response takes definite action now to change the probability and/or the impact of a threat, leaving some residual risk (see manual 9.2.3.1). Testing in every sprint and an interim audit make late failures less likely and less damaging but cannot rule them out.

n.0: Avoid makes the threat certain not to happen, for example by removing its cause; testing lowers the likelihood, but the final audit could still find failures.
n.2: Transfer passes part of the financial impact to a third party; having the supplier test does not move the impact of a missed go-live date.
n.3: A contingent plan is prepared now and used if the risk occurs; the sprint testing and interim audit are planned to take place in any case.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. In a risk workshop, Kestrel Lane's team says that moving 26,000 existing permits from the old database is low risk because their past migrations for other clients have gone well. Nobody challenges this, and the risk is scored as low probability without examining the quality of the council's old data. Is this an effective way to apply the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because Kestrel Lane is the supplier and is best placed to judge the risks in its own technical work.
Yes, because a risk workshop with the team is a recognized way to identify and assess the project's risks.
No, because migration risks belong to the business layer and should be recorded in its own register.
No, because optimism and groupthink may be hiding the risk, and data on the old records should inform the score.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Risk assessment can be distorted by decision bias such as optimism bias and groupthink, and data and analytics should be used to identify and assess risks (see manual 9.2.4 and 9.3.2.6). Testing a sample of the council's old records would give evidence for the probability score.

n.0: Supplier expertise is valuable, but success for other clients is not evidence about this council's data, and an unchallenged view is a sign of bias.
n.1: Workshops are a valid technique, but this one accepted an untested assumption, so the assessment is not effective.
n.2: The migration is project work; its risks are managed in the project's risk register.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: The council's leadership team has a very low appetite for risks to residents' personal data. In the 'initiating a project' process, Hannah Okoro drafts the risk management approach. It proposes that the project board sets a tight risk tolerance for data protection, so that any data risk still assessed above 'low' after its response is escalated to the board straight away. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project manager sets the risk appetite for the project when writing the approach.
Yes, because the board sets risk tolerances from the business's appetite, and the approach says how they are applied.
No, because risk appetite and risk tolerance should both be set by the leadership team, not the project board.
No, because the specific data risks and their scores belong in the risk management approach itself.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Risk appetite is set by the business; risk tolerance is a measurable threshold set by the project board based on that appetite, and the risk management approach describes the procedures, techniques and responsibilities for managing risk on the project (see manual 9.2.1).

n.0: Risk appetite belongs to the business, here the leadership team; the project manager applies it but does not set it.
n.2: The business sets the appetite, but the risk tolerance for the project is set by the project board based on that appetite.
n.3: The risk management approach describes how risk is managed and holds no specific risks; individual risks go in the risk register.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage. At a sprint review, Tom Achebe reports that the payment page will not meet WCAG 2.2 AA, a quality specification in its product description, because of the card payment component used. Fixing it would need two extra sprints. How should Hannah Okoro classify this issue, and why?
o: As an off-specification, because a product is forecast not to meet one of its quality specifications.
As a request for change, because Kestrel Lane is asking for two more sprints to rework the payment page.
As a concern, because the effect of the failure on the go-live date has not yet been assessed.
As a risk, because the page might still pass the independent audit after further work in later sprints.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet, or is forecast not to meet, its quality specifications (see manual 10.2.3). It is handled through change control: the fix is approved, or a concession granted, by the board or the change authority.

n.1: A request for change proposes altering a baseline; here the baseline is unchanged and the product is failing to meet it.
n.2: Every issue is assessed for impact; the failure has already been found, so the more specific type, off-specification, applies.
n.3: The failure is already known, so it is an issue rather than an uncertain future event.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Permits Online is in the 'initiating a project' process. Graham Pell proposes that Tom Achebe, Kestrel Lane's delivery manager, act as change authority for every request for change, with no cost limit and no change budget, because his team knows the backlog best. Is this an effective way to apply the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project board may delegate the approval of requests for change to a change authority.
Yes, because under a time-and-materials contract the supplier pays for any changes that it approves.
No, because delegated change authority should have defined limits, with a change budget, set by the board.
No, because the project board must decide every request for change itself and cannot delegate this.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The board is the ultimate authority for requests for change but may delegate approval to a change authority within defined limits, ideally with a change budget so that approved changes can be funded (see manual 10.2.4 and 10.2.5). Unlimited authority for the supplier's delivery manager removes the board's control over the baseline and over a capped contract.

n.0: Delegation is allowed, but within defined limits; unlimited authority with no budget is not effective delegation.
n.1: Under time and materials the council pays for the time used, so changes approved by the supplier would raise the council's costs.
n.3: The board may delegate approval of changes to a change authority or to the project manager.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Permits Online is in the discovery and alpha stage. This is Hannah Okoro's first project of this size, and Calderbrook has little experience of PRINCE2 or of working with an agile supplier. The board asks for a highlight report every week during this stage, moving to every two weeks once it is confident that reporting is reliable. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because weekly highlight reports mean that the board need not set tolerances for this stage.
Yes, because reporting frequency should match the control needed, and can be reduced as confidence grows.
No, because highlight reports are produced at the end of each stage to support the decision on the next stage.
No, because the frequency of highlight reports is set by the team manager in each work package description.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The frequency of reporting should reflect the level of control needed: inexperience calls for more frequent reports until confidence grows (see manual 11.2.4). The board sets the interval for highlight reports.

n.0: Reports inform the board but do not replace tolerances, which define the authority delegated to the project manager.
n.2: That describes the end stage report; highlight reports are time-driven reports at intervals set by the board.
n.3: Work package descriptions set checkpoint reporting from team manager to project manager; the board sets highlight report frequency.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Permits Online is in the private beta stage, which has a time tolerance of two weeks. A delay in the ICT team's integration work means Hannah Okoro forecasts the stage will finish six days late. She moves a testing work package earlier to recover some time, records the issue and reports both in her next highlight report. Is this an effective way to apply the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the forecast is within stage tolerance, so she can take corrective action and report it routinely.
Yes, because the business layer sets stage tolerances and will be told if they are breached.
No, because a delay affecting a fixed go-live date should be escalated to the board in an exception report.
No, because Alan Briggs, as manager of the delayed team, should raise an exception report to the board.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: An exception is a forecast breach of tolerance. While the stage is forecast to finish within its tolerance, the project manager takes corrective action and reports through highlight reports; an exception report is needed when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded (see manual 11.2.6 and 16.4.6).

n.1: The project board, not the business layer, sets stage tolerances.
n.2: The go-live date matters, but the stage is still forecast within the tolerance the board set, so there is no exception to escalate.
n.3: Problems at team level are raised with the project manager as issues; exception reports go from the project manager to the board.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (risk). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is recording risk information as it moves from starting up into initiation and delivery. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: During starting up, before any registers have been set up, Leah Whitfield notes a possible threat that contamination under the warehouse floor could delay the structural works.
o: Risk register
Daily log
Issue management approach
Risk management approach
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: In starting up a project, an initial set of key risks is identified and recorded in the daily log, because the risk register is not set up until initiation (manual table 13.3 and 4.3.2).

n.0: The risk register is set up in initiating a project; until then early risks are kept in the daily log.
n.2: The issue management approach describes how issues and changes are handled; it holds no specific risks.
n.3: The risk management approach describes procedures and scales and contains no specific risks; it is also not written until initiation.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (risk). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is recording risk information as it moves from starting up into initiation and delivery. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: In initiation, Leah Whitfield sets out the five-point probability and impact scales the project will use, and that threats scoring 15 or more will be reported to the board.
o: Risk register
Daily log
Issue management approach
Risk management approach
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The risk management approach describes how risk will be managed: the procedures, techniques, standards and responsibilities, such as scoring scales and when risks are escalated (manual 9.2.1 and chapter 9 products).

n.0: The risk register records specific risks and their status, not the scales and procedure for assessing them.
n.1: These are agreed procedures for the whole project, not informal notes.
n.2: Probability and impact scales for risks belong in the risk management approach, not the approach for issues and change control.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (risk). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is recording risk information as it moves from starting up into initiation and delivery. Which product should each piece of information be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: In stage 2, Leah Whitfield records that, as the Danish manufacturer has a full order book, the rig may be delivered late, delaying the opening, with Sunita Rao as risk owner.
o: Risk register
Daily log
Issue management approach
Risk management approach
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The risk register records each identified risk with its description as cause, event and effect, its owner and its status (manual chapter 9 products).

n.1: Once the risk register exists, formal risks are recorded there with an owner, not in the daily log.
n.2: This is a specific uncertain event, not a procedure for handling issues.
n.3: The risk management approach holds procedures and scales, never individual risks.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (issues). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage, and Leah Whitfield is recording new issues in the issue register. Which type of issue should each be recorded as? Statement 1 of 3: Craig Dunmore asks for the plant room to be enlarged so that the heat pumps are easier to maintain, which would change the approved design.
o: Off-specification
Request for change
Business opportunity
Event external to the project
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline, here the approved design (manual 10.1 and issue types).

n.0: Nothing has failed to meet its specification; Craig wants the specification itself changed.
n.2: This is a proposed change to the baseline, not an unexpected positive consequence for the organization.
n.3: The request comes from within the project team about its own design, not from an event outside the project.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (issues). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage, and Leah Whitfield is recording new issues in the issue register. Which type of issue should each be recorded as? Statement 2 of 3: Testing shows that the electrical installation in two classrooms will not meet the earthing specification in its product description.
o: Off-specification
Request for change
Business opportunity
Event external to the project
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications (manual 10.1 and issue types).

n.1: No one is proposing to change the baseline; the product is forecast to fall short of it.
n.2: A shortfall against specification is not a positive opportunity.
n.3: The failure is in the project's own product, not an event outside the project.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (issues). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage, and Leah Whitfield is recording new issues in the issue register. Which type of issue should each be recorded as? Statement 3 of 3: Bethany Cole points out that the welding bays could also host paid evening courses for local adults, bringing the college extra income.
o: Off-specification
Request for change
Business opportunity
Event external to the project
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: A business opportunity is an unanticipated positive consequence for the project or the user organization, here extra income for the college (manual 10.1 and issue types).

n.0: No product is failing to meet its specification.
n.1: No change to an approved product is proposed; the idea is a new way for the college to benefit.
n.3: The idea comes from within the project, from a user, not from an event outside it.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (progress). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 1 of 3: Leah Whitfield's monthly summary to the board of the stage's status, including site safety incidents, as one governor has asked.
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
Lessons log
End stage report
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The highlight report is the project manager's regular, time-driven summary of stage status to the project board, at an interval the board sets (manual chapter 11 products).

n.1: Checkpoint reports go from a team manager to the project manager about a work package.
n.2: This is a status report to the board, not a note of a lesson.
n.3: The end stage report is produced once, at the end of the stage, not every month.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (progress). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 2 of 3: Leah Whitfield notes that the contractor's weekly written reports give a far clearer picture of progress than the verbal reports on the lab refurbishment did.
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
Lessons log
End stage report
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The lessons log is the informal repository for lessons that could be applied on this or future projects (manual chapter 11 products).

n.0: The observation is a lesson about reporting, not a summary of stage status for the board.
n.1: A checkpoint report gives work package status; this is a lesson learned.
n.3: Lessons may later feed the end stage report, but the note is first recorded in the lessons log.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (progress). Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the asbestos removal, strip-out and structural works stage. Which report or log should each item be recorded in? Statement 3 of 3: At the end of the stage, Leah Whitfield summarizes its performance and the overall project position so the board can decide whether to authorize the fit-out stage.
o: Highlight report
Checkpoint report
Lessons log
End stage report
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The end stage report, produced in managing a stage boundary, summarizes the stage's progress and the overall project situation so the board can decide what to do next (manual chapter 11 products).

n.0: Highlight reports are routine during a stage; the event-driven report at the stage end is the end stage report.
n.1: Checkpoint reports cover a work package, not the stage and the project.
n.2: This is a formal report to the board, not an informal record of lessons.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. There is a risk that the nacelle rig, with its 30-week lead time, arrives after opening day. Leah Whitfield agrees with Ade Okafor that, if this happens, first-term apprentices will train on Brackmoor's own rig at its base, and she sets aside money in the risk budget for transport, to be spent if the rig is late. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because it is a transfer response, passing the financial impact of a late rig to Brackmoor Offshore Wind.
Yes, because it prepares a contingent plan now, funded by the risk budget, for use if the risk occurs.
No, because money for responding to risks should come from the change budget rather than the risk budget.
No, because late delivery depends on a supplier in Denmark, so the risk should be accepted and watched.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Preparing contingent plans means planning actions now that will be used only if the risk occurs; the risk budget funds specific responses to risks, such as contingent plans (see manual 9.2.3.1 and table 9.1).

n.0: Transfer passes the financial impact to a third party such as an insurer; here the college plans actions and pays for them itself.
n.2: The change budget funds approved changes; responses to risks, including contingent plans, are funded from the risk budget.
n.3: A risk outside the project's direct control can still have a response planned; acceptance is one option, not a requirement.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. At a risk workshop, Craig Dunmore raises the threat of a site vehicle striking a student on the pedestrian route. The group rates it as very unlikely because the expected contractor has worked safely for the college before, and Mark Ostrowski says he does not want safety worries to delay the start. Nobody challenges this, and the threat is accepted with no action. Is this an effective way to apply the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because data on past performance predicts future performance and so supports the low rating.
Yes, because the project board sets risk tolerance, so the workshop can accept threats that fall within it.
No, because optimism bias and groupthink are distorting the assessment, despite the lab project's vehicle incident.
No, because threats to safety should be transferred to the contractor through the design-and-build contract.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Decision bias can harm risk management: optimism bias discounts unfavourable risks and assumes success, and groupthink values group cohesion over dissent (see manual 9.2.4). The lab refurbishment's reportable incident with a contractor's van shows the threat is real, so the assessment and response need to be revisited.

n.0: Past data can help, but here it is used selectively: the college's own last project had a reportable vehicle incident.
n.1: Tolerance is set by the board, but that does not excuse an assessment distorted by bias.
n.3: Transfer deals with the financial impact; it does not remove the need for an honest assessment and suitable action on a safety threat.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design and procurement stage. Sunita Rao asks for 30 welding bays instead of 24. Leah Whitfield records it as a request for change, assesses with Hamish Grant and the architect its effect on cost, space, fume extraction, timescale and the business case, and sends the board an issue report setting out options, a recommendation and the consequences of approving or rejecting it. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the vice principal is the senior user and can approve changes to user requirements herself.
Yes, because the request is captured and assessed, then a recommendation goes to those with authority to decide.
No, because a request raised informally by a board member should be recorded in the daily log instead.
No, because a request that adds cost must be escalated to the board in an exception report.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The issues technique captures the issue, assesses its effect on targets, the business case and other products, recommends options to whoever holds the authority with the consequences of each made clear, then records the decision and implements it (see manual 10.3.1).

n.0: The senior user represents the users, but requests for change are decided by the board or a delegated change authority.
n.2: A request to change the approved design needs formal handling in the issue register, however it was raised.
n.3: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance; a request for change is presented in an issue report.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The board delegates to Leah Whitfield the authority to approve requests for change costing up to £10,000 each. It does not set a change budget, saying that approved changes can be paid for from the risk budget held for asbestos and ground conditions. Is this an effective way to apply the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the board is the ultimate authority for changes and may delegate approval to the project manager.
Yes, because one shared budget gives Leah more flexibility to deal with the asbestos and ground risks.
No, because the project manager cannot be a change authority, as approving changes is a board role.
No, because delegated change authority needs a change budget, and the risk budget is for responses to risks.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The board may delegate authority to approve changes, but it should come with a change budget so that approved changes can be funded and implemented; the risk budget is for responses to risks, not for changes (see manual 10.2.4, 10.2.5 and chapter 9).

n.0: Delegation to the project manager is allowed, but without a change budget the approved changes cannot properly be funded.
n.1: Spending the risk budget on changes would leave the asbestos and ground risks without the funds set aside for them.
n.2: The board may delegate approval of changes to a change authority or to the project manager.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the commissioning and handover stage. On a walk-round, instructors make 60 minor comments, such as scuffed paint and a sticking cupboard door, all of which the contractor has agreed to put right under the contract. Leah Whitfield records each one as a formal issue in the issue register and prepares an issue report on each for the board. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because comments from instructors are concerns, and each concern should be assessed and decided by the board.
Yes, because a full record of every snag will be needed for the end project report at closure.
No, because judgement is needed on what to record formally, and minor snags under the contract can be handled informally.
No, because snagging items are risks rather than issues and should go in the risk register.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Judgement is needed on which issues to record formally: too many trivial issues swamp decision-making, and informal issues can be managed in the daily log (see manual 10.2.2 and 10.1). Minor snags the contractor is already obliged to fix do not need board decisions.

n.0: Concerns are assessed by the project manager first; the board decides on issues beyond the project manager's authority.
n.1: The end project report reviews products and off-specifications; it does not need each minor snag raised formally.
n.3: The snags already exist, so they are not uncertain events; they are minor issues.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The finance and resources committee meets every two months but wants to know at once about any forecast overspend. Leah Whitfield agrees monthly highlight reports for the board and weekly written checkpoint reports from the contractor. She also agrees to send an exception report as soon as a stage is forecast to exceed its cost tolerance, and Mark Ostrowski will pass any forecast project overspend to the committee. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because regular time-driven reports are combined with event-driven escalation when a breach is forecast.
Yes, because highlight reports should go straight to the finance and resources committee instead of the board.
No, because exception reports should be timed to match the committee's meetings every two months.
No, because weekly checkpoint reports are more frequent than a project of this size needs.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Progress control combines time-driven controls, such as highlight and checkpoint reports at agreed intervals, with event-driven controls, such as an exception report raised as soon as a breach of tolerance is forecast (see manual 11.2.2 and 11.2.6).

n.1: Highlight reports go to the project board; the committee, as part of the business layer, is told about project-level exceptions.
n.2: Exception reporting is event-driven: it happens as soon as a breach is forecast, not at fixed intervals.
n.3: Reporting frequency reflects the control needed; written weekly reports also address the lab project's lesson about verbal reporting.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Tarnside's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the mechanical and electrical fit-out stage. Heat pump prices have risen, and Leah Whitfield's exception report forecasts that the project will finish 5% over budget, beyond the governors' 3% limit. Mark Ostrowski asks her to prepare an exception plan funded by a further £150,000 from college reserves, and the board approves it at its next meeting without referring it to the governors. Is this an effective way to apply the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the project board decides how to respond to exception reports raised by the project manager.
Yes, because Mark Ostrowski controls the college's reserves and so can provide the extra funding.
No, because the exception plan should have been prepared before the exception report was sent to the board.
No, because a forecast breach of project tolerance is for the business layer, here the governors, to decide.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Under exception management the board decides on forecast breaches of stage tolerance, but forecast breaches of project tolerance are decided by the business layer, which set those tolerances (see manual 11.2.1 and 11.3.1). Here the governors set the 3% limit, so they must decide.

n.0: The board decides on breaches of stage tolerance; a forecast breach of project tolerance goes to the business layer.
n.1: Controlling reserves does not give the executive authority to exceed tolerances set by the governors.
n.2: The exception report comes first; the board then decides whether to request an exception plan.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (risk). At different points in the SPA project, Ellie Chandran needs to record the following. Where should each be recorded? Statement 1 of 3: In the 'starting up a project' process, before any registers have been set up, she notes an early threat that the union may delay agreement of the new rotas.
o: Risk management approach
Risk register
Daily log
Issue register
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: In starting up a project, an initial set of key risks is identified and recorded in the daily log until the risk register exists (see manual table 13.3).

n.0: The risk management approach sets out procedures, scales and responsibilities; it does not hold specific risks.
n.1: The risk register is set up in initiation; until then, early risks are noted in the daily log.
n.3: This is an uncertain future event, so it is a risk rather than an issue.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (risk). At different points in the SPA project, Ellie Chandran needs to record the following. Where should each be recorded? Statement 2 of 3: In the design stage: because several Moorside GP practices may keep faxing referrals to nurses they know, referrals could bypass triage and first contact could be delayed. Moira Healy will own the risk.
o: Risk management approach
Risk register
Daily log
Issue register
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Identified risks, described by cause, event and effect and with their owner, are recorded in the risk register, which holds each risk's status and history (see manual chapter 9).

n.0: The risk management approach describes how risks will be managed; it does not contain specific risks.
n.2: Once the risk register exists, risks are recorded there rather than in the daily log.
n.3: No referral has yet been delayed; the delay is an uncertain future event, so it is a risk.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (risk). At different points in the SPA project, Ellie Chandran needs to record the following. Where should each be recorded? Statement 3 of 3: In the design stage: Medivault confirms that its configuration team will start three weeks later than agreed, and she decides the delay needs formal handling.
o: Risk management approach
Risk register
Daily log
Issue register
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The late start has already been confirmed, so it is an issue rather than a risk, and formal issues are recorded in the issue register (see manual 10.1).

n.0: The risk management approach holds procedures, not specific risks or issues.
n.1: The late start is confirmed rather than uncertain; something that has already happened is an issue.
n.2: Informal issues can be kept in the daily log, but Ellie has decided that this one needs formal handling.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (issues). The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage, and Ellie Chandran is capturing new issues. Which type of issue is each of the following? Statement 1 of 3: The patients' forum asks for carers to be able to refer patients directly through the SPA, which is not in the approved scope.
o: Request for change
Problem
External event
Off-specification
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline; direct referral by carers would change the approved scope (see manual 10.1).

n.1: A problem is something already having a negative effect on the project; this is a proposal to add to the scope.
n.2: This is a proposal from a stakeholder to change what the project delivers, not an outside event whose effect must be assessed.
n.3: Nothing delivered has failed its specification; the forum wants something added.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (issues). The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage, and Ellie Chandran is capturing new issues. Which type of issue is each of the following? Statement 2 of 3: Testing shows that the configured e-referral form does not capture the referrer's contact number, which its product description requires.
o: Request for change
Problem
External event
Off-specification
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications (see manual 10.1).

n.0: Nobody is proposing to change the baseline; the product fails to meet its agreed specification.
n.1: The fault has a negative effect, but the specific type for a product that will not meet its specification is off-specification.
n.2: The fault is in a product the project is delivering, not in an event outside the project.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (issues). The SPA project is in the design and pilot preparation stage, and Ellie Chandran is capturing new issues. Which type of issue is each of the following? Statement 3 of 3: The government publishes new national guidance on community nursing referrals, which may affect the triage criteria.
o: Request for change
Problem
External event
Off-specification
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: An event outside the project that may affect it is captured as an issue of that type and then assessed (see manual 10.1).

n.0: Nobody has yet proposed a change; the effect of the guidance first needs to be assessed.
n.1: The guidance is not known to be causing harm; it is an outside event whose effect must be assessed.
n.3: No product has been found to fail its specification.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (progress). The trust's executive team has set project tolerances of plus or minus 10% on cost and one month on time; beyond those, the trust board decides. Which role should decide how to respond to each situation? Statement 1 of 3: During the roll-out, the Moorside go-live is forecast to slip so far that the project will finish six weeks after its target date.
o: Business layer
Project board
Project manager
Team manager
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: A forecast breach of project tolerance, here one month on time, is outside the project board's authority and is decided by the business layer, which set the project tolerances (see manual 11.2.1 and 11.3.1).

n.1: The board decides on stage-level exceptions; a forecast breach of project tolerance goes to the business layer.
n.2: The project manager escalates exceptions to the board; deciding on a project-level exception is not within her authority.
n.3: The team manager works within work package tolerances and escalates to the project manager.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (progress). The trust's executive team has set project tolerances of plus or minus 10% on cost and one month on time; beyond those, the trust board decides. Which role should decide how to respond to each situation? Statement 2 of 3: Josie Barker forecasts that her configuration work package will finish three days beyond its time tolerance, though the stage is still forecast to finish within its tolerances.
o: Business layer
Project board
Project manager
Team manager
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The project manager sets work package tolerances; a forecast breach is raised by the team manager as an issue and handled by the project manager in controlling a stage (see manual 11.2.1 and 11.2.6).

n.0: Project tolerances are not threatened, so the business layer is not involved.
n.1: Exceptions to stage or project plans go to the board; this one is at work package level.
n.3: The team manager raises the forecast breach with the project manager rather than deciding on it herself.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: Matching set (progress). The trust's executive team has set project tolerances of plus or minus 10% on cost and one month on time; beyond those, the trust board decides. Which role should decide how to respond to each situation? Statement 3 of 3: Ellie Chandran forecasts that the Eastfield pilot stage will exceed its cost tolerance, although the project as a whole is still forecast to stay within 10%.
o: Business layer
Project board
Project manager
Team manager
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The project board sets stage tolerances and decides how to respond to an exception report about a forecast breach of them, for example by asking for an exception plan (see manual 11.2.1 and 11.3.1).

n.0: Project tolerances are not forecast to be breached, so the business layer does not need to decide.
n.2: The project manager cannot authorize work beyond stage tolerance; she escalates it to the board in an exception report.
n.3: The team manager has no authority over stage tolerances.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. At a risk workshop attended mostly by Eastfield staff, Moira Healy, who is widely respected, rates the risk that Moorside nurses will not adopt the triage hub as low, and nobody challenges her. Ellie Chandran is concerned that the group is agreeing too readily, so she holds a second session with Gareth Pugh and two Moorside nurses and asks them how the hub could fail. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because groupthink can distort the assessment of risks, and dissenting views help to counter it.
Yes, because risks should be identified by people outside the project team rather than by its own members.
No, because the risk has already been assessed as low and should now be accepted and monitored.
No, because the risk owner assesses the risk, and Moira Healy has already given her assessment of it.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: PRINCE2 7 recognizes that decision bias can distort risk decisions; groupthink values agreement within a group over dissent or the right answer (see manual 9.2.4). Seeking the views of people likely to disagree, here the Moorside nurses most affected, is a practical counter-measure.

n.1: Project team members are a main source of risk identification; the point here is to widen the range of views, not to exclude the team.
n.2: An assessment made under bias is unreliable; reassessing it is part of managing the risk.
n.3: A risk owner manages the response to a risk; that does not make one person's rating final, especially when bias is suspected.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The trust has a low appetite for risk to clinical safety and a moderate appetite for risk to administrative processes. Ellie Chandran's draft risk management approach uses one set of scales and one risk tolerance for every risk, so a threat that a triage criterion might miss a red-flag symptom is handled in the same way as a threat that a rota spreadsheet is late. Is this an effective way to apply the risk practice, and why?
o: Yes, because a single set of scales keeps risk scoring simple for a project manager who is new to PRINCE2 7.
Yes, because risk appetite is set by the business, so the project's own approach does not need to reflect it.
No, because the risk management approach should list each clinical safety risk together with its owner and its response.
No, because the board should set risk tolerances that reflect the trust's different appetites for clinical and administrative risk.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Risk appetite is set by the business, and risk tolerance, a measurable threshold for each objective at risk, is set by the project board based on that appetite (see manual 9.2.1). A trust with a low appetite for clinical safety risk needs tighter thresholds and faster escalation for those risks than for administrative ones.

n.0: Simplicity helps, but treating clinical safety risks like administrative ones disregards the trust's stated appetite.
n.1: The appetite is set by the business precisely so that the board can set tolerances that apply it.
n.2: Specific risks, owners and responses go in the risk register; the approach sets procedures, scales and responsibilities.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: The SPA project is in the Eastfield pilot stage. The patients' forum's request for carers to refer directly has been captured as an issue. Ellie Chandran assesses that it would cost £8,000 and add a week, within the stage tolerances, but the board has not delegated any authority to her to approve changes. What should Ellie produce to obtain a decision, and why?
o: An exception report, because the request falls outside the approved scope of the project.
A highlight report entry, because the cost and delay can be met within the stage tolerances.
An updated work package description, so that the change can be passed to the team manager.
An issue report, setting out the impact of the request and recommending a decision to the board.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: An issue report describes an issue's impact on the baseline, sets out options and recommends a decision; it is used for requests for change that need a formal decision. Within tolerance, an issue report rather than an exception report is the right product (see manual 10.2.3 and 10.3.1).

n.0: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance; this change is within tolerance.
n.1: Staying within tolerance does not give Ellie authority to approve a change; the board has kept that authority.
n.2: Work packages are updated after a change is approved; no decision has yet been made.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: The SPA project is in the 'initiating a project' process. The board proposes that Ellie Chandran may approve requests for change costing up to £5,000 each, from a change budget of £30,000. Any request affecting the triage criteria must first be signed off by the clinical safety officer and the medical director and then go to the board for a decision. Is this an effective way to apply the issues practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the change budget can also pay for responses to clinical safety risks found during the pilot.
Yes, because delegating minor changes with a budget speeds decisions, while clinically sensitive ones go higher.
No, because the project board is the change authority, and so it may not delegate the approval of changes.
No, because a change authority should also carry out the changes it approves through its own work packages.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The board is the ultimate authority for requests for change but may delegate approval, within limits, to a change authority or the project manager, with a change budget so that approved changes can be funded (see manual 10.2.4 and 10.2.5). Keeping changes to triage criteria at board level, after clinical sign-off, respects the trust's low appetite for clinical safety risk.

n.0: Responses to risks are funded from a risk budget; the change budget funds approved changes.
n.2: The board may delegate approval of changes within limits; it remains the ultimate authority.
n.3: Delegation concerns approving changes; approved changes are implemented through work packages authorized by the project manager.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: The SPA project is close to the end of the Eastfield pilot stage. Ellie Chandran needs to give the board a summary of how the pilot stage performed, the overall position of the project and enough information for the board to decide whether to go ahead with the roll-out. Which product should she prepare, and why?
o: A highlight report, because it gives the board a regular summary of the stage's status at the interval the board set.
A lessons report, because the trust board has asked for a written record of what the project learns as it goes.
An end stage report, because it reviews the stage and the project's position so the board can decide what to do next.
An exception report, because the board must decide whether to change the plan for the roll-out stage.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: The end stage report, prepared when evaluating the stage near its end, summarizes progress to date and the overall project situation and gives the board the information it needs to decide what to do next (see manual chapter 11 and chapter 18).

n.0: Highlight reports are time-driven updates during the stage; the decision to go ahead is supported by the event-driven end stage report.
n.1: A lessons report passes on lessons; it does not give the stage summary the board needs for the next-stage decision.
n.3: An exception report is used when a plan is forecast to exceed tolerance; nothing here says tolerances are threatened.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: The SPA project is in the Eastfield pilot stage. The triage hub team has just been formed and has never worked to a work package before, while Medivault's configuration team has switched on the same referral module for other providers. Ellie Chandran sets weekly checkpoint reports in the hub work package and fortnightly ones in Medivault's. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because reporting should be more frequent for an inexperienced team until confidence in its work grows.
Yes, because Medivault is an external supplier, so it reports to the senior supplier rather than to the project manager.
No, because checkpoint reports should be at the same interval in every work package so the highlight report is consistent.
No, because the frequency of checkpoint reports is set by the project board in the communication management approach.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Reporting frequency should reflect the level of control needed: an inexperienced team reports more often until confidence grows, an experienced one less often (see manual 11.2.4). Checkpoint frequency is set in each work package description.

n.1: Checkpoint reports go from the team manager to the project manager, whoever the supplier is.
n.2: Each work package sets its own reporting frequency; the highlight report draws them together whatever their intervals.
n.3: The board sets the interval for highlight reports; checkpoint frequency is agreed in the work package between the project manager and the team manager.

Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.q: The SPA project is in the evaluation and roll-out stage. Ellie Chandran has been compiling progress by hand from 14 spreadsheets. She now has the e-rostering and training systems feed data automatically into a weekly progress view showing referral routes switched over, staff trained and triage shifts filled, which board members can open on their phones. Is this an effective way to apply the progress practice, and why?
o: Yes, because the system can then set each locality's tolerances from its own past performance.
Yes, because data and systems can remove manual collation and present progress in the format people prefer.
No, because highlight reports are written by the project manager and should not draw on automated data.
No, because these figures measure benefits, which are reviewed after the project has closed.
Practitioner: Risk, Issues & Progress.w: Using data and systems in progress management can remove manual consolidation of separate sources, use past performance to help forecast and present progress in the format stakeholders prefer (see manual 11.2.7).
